title: The Inconvenient Figure
body: Your division's flagship scheme is reviewed every quarter by the Permanent Secretary, and this quarter's figure is bad: only 31% of the people eligible for it are using it. A number that low gets a scheme cut. {senior} asks, mildly, whether it might be "presented as a range rather than a number".

choices.text: Present it as a range.
choices.outcome: The slide says "30-60%", and nobody at the review asks how a range that wide was arrived at. {senior} never mentions it again, which you decide to take as approval. The real figure stays in your files.

choices.text: Present the number.
choices.outcome: You present 31%. The review runs forty minutes over, and the scheme is sent for a full redesign with your slide attached. {senior} doesn't invite you to the next meeting, or the four after that.

choices.text: Present the number, with a recovery plan attached.
choices.outcome: You give up the weekend for eleven slides nobody asked for: the number, and how to fix it. {senior} presents them as {senior.their} own. The scheme survives. So do you.

title: The Report
body: Your ministry paid a consultancy $1.9 million to work out why one of its schemes isn't working. Today they present their final deck, and it's your own idea: the one you set out in a minute paper, a memo to the people above you asking for a decision, which nobody acted on. Only your paragraph four, on how it could go wrong, is missing. The Deputy Secretary who hired them loves it.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let them have it.
choices.outcome: The recommendation is adopted with enthusiasm. At the townhall it's described as "a fresh external perspective", and you clap with everyone else.

choices.text: Circulate your old minute paper.
choices.outcome: You send the minute paper, paragraph four and all, to the fourteen people at the presentation. Nobody replies except a Deputy Secretary you've never met, who writes only to you: "Good paper." The one who hired the consultants reads it too.

choices.text: Ask the consultants, in the Q&A, what their data source was.
choices.outcome: The consultancy's partner checks the appendix and reads out the source: a minute paper from your division, written before the consultants were hired. Yours. The room enjoys this more than the partner does.

title: Public Sector Transformation
body: Your division has been sent on a two-day offsite to plan its "transformation", and {peer} is at your table. Each table has to fill post-its with ways to make the division "more agile, more citizen-centric and more data-driven", with no extra staff or money. The best post-its go into a deck for the Permanent Secretary.

choices.text: Write down what everyone is actually thinking.
choices.outcome: Your post-it says "We need three more officers." {peer} sticks one beside it that says "Agree." Neither makes it into the deck. The Deputy Secretary running the offsite asks, pleasantly, whose handwriting that was.

choices.text: Produce an acronym.
choices.outcome: You offer S.E.R.V.E. The facilitator writes it up in green marker, and it's on a banner in the lift lobby for the next six years. Nobody ever agrees on what the second E stands for.

choices.text: Volunteer to write the follow-up implementation plan.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted it. Your plan gives every idea an owner and a date, and it's the only document from the offsite that anyone opens twice. The transformation is now, quietly, yours.

variants.title: Design Thinking
variants.body: Your division is spending a day on a design-thinking sprint to redesign one of its services. The wall has a map of the citizen's journey and an imaginary user called "Auntie Mary". The facilitator asks everyone to stick their assumptions in a box marked PARKING LOT. Whatever survives the day becomes next year's plan.

choices.text: Park the assumption everyone actually has.
choices.outcome: You write "No new resources" on a sticky note and put it in the parking lot. The facilitator laughs, stops laughing, and moves it to a corner. The Deputy Secretary who paid for the facilitator watches it go.

choices.text: Give Auntie Mary a tagline.
choices.outcome: You offer "Auntie Mary: Served Once, Served Right." It's printed on a tote bag, and for years you see the tote bag at hawker centres, carried by people who were never at the sprint.

choices.text: Volunteer to turn the wall into a plan.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted the wall. Your plan is the only thing from the sprint that outlives the sprint, and so, without anyone deciding it, the redesign becomes yours.

variants.title: The Retreat
variants.body: The ministry is holding a two-day retreat at a Sentosa hotel to agree its new values, and every officer has to join a breakout room. The rooms are named after the old values. You're in Integrity, the room with no window. Each room reports one idea back to the Permanent Secretary at five.

choices.text: Say what the division actually needs: more officers.
choices.outcome: You say the division needs three more officers, not a fourth value. The room agrees in silence, and the scribe doesn't write it down. Your point reaches the Permanent Secretary anyway, because the scribe repeats it over coffee.

choices.text: Propose a new value.
choices.outcome: You propose "Ownership with Heart". It's adopted by the afternoon, and by the end of the quarter it's printed on every lanyard in the ministry, including yours.

choices.text: Volunteer to write up the retreat.
choices.outcome: You write it up properly, with an owner and a date for every action. It's the first retreat report anyone has acted on, and you're now, somehow, in charge of all of it.

variants.body: Your division spends a day imagining four possible futures for Singapore in 2060, so that it can plan for all of them. The facilitator's one rule is that nobody says "budget" before lunch. By eleven you notice that all four futures have your division in them, with exactly today's staff.

choices.text: Say "budget" at 11:15.
choices.outcome: You point out that all four futures assume today's headcount. The facilitator writes "resourcing" on the whiteboard outside all four futures, in a corner that belongs to none of them, and the Deputy Secretary at the back makes a note.

choices.text: Give the four futures names.
choices.outcome: You call them Harbour, Haze, Heartland and Hive. The names outlive the exercise by a decade. Hive turns up years later in a Minister's speech, meaning something else entirely.

choices.text: Volunteer to write up the implications.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted to. Your paper turns four futures into six actions, each with an owner and a date. Two of them happen within the year: the only part of 2060 to arrive early.

variants.title: The Innovation Challenge
variants.body: Your division is running an innovation challenge: five teams pitch for five minutes each, and a panel of three directors gives the winner $5,000 to build a prototype. Winning gets a team noticed upstairs. Your team's idea is good. The team before yours has a logo.

choices.text: Pitch the real problem: the team is short of people.
choices.outcome: You spend your five minutes on headcount. The panel thanks you for your candour and gives the grant to the logo. Your slide turns up, without your name on it, at the next directors' retreat.

choices.text: Give your idea a logo, and an acronym.
choices.outcome: Your idea becomes S.P.A.R.K. and wins by one vote. The panel's chair hands over the cheque and asks what it stands for. Nobody on your team can remember.

choices.text: Offer to build whichever idea wins.
choices.outcome: The logo wins, and its team moves straight on to next year's challenge. Over the next year you quietly build their idea. Version two, the one that actually works, is yours.

title: A Word You Have Not Heard Before
body: Over lunch, a friend who works in HR mentions your "CEP" as if you'd know the term. You don't, so your friend explains: Currently Estimated Potential, HR's private estimate of the highest grade you'll ever reach, set early in your career and never told to you. Your friend has clearly seen yours, and changes the subject to the new chicken rice stall downstairs.

choices.text: Ask what yours says.
choices.outcome: Your friend won't tell you the grade, and says only, very quietly, that it's reviewed every year and can still move. You think about it in the lift, and on most days after that.

choices.text: Let it go.
choices.outcome: You let it go, and try the chicken rice. You'll hear the term again years from now, in a sentence that begins "Well, realistically".

title: The Nomination
body: Your division can put one name forward this year for the Public Service Leadership Programme, the course that marks people out for the top jobs. {senior} wants your nomination by Friday, and it can be your own name. Everyone expects you to put forward the division's scholar, one of the high-flyers the government paid to study overseas, who is going places anyway.

choices.text: Nominate yourself.
choices.outcome: It isn't done, putting your own name forward. It also isn't forbidden. {senior} writes your name down slowly, and a committee you'll never meet raises its estimate of how far you'll go.

choices.text: Nominate the obvious scholar.
choices.outcome: The scholar was going anyway, and thanks you, warmly and sincerely, which somehow makes it worse. The officer who does the division's real work reads the shortlist on the intranet, like everyone else.

choices.text: Nominate the quiet officer who does all the actual work.
choices.outcome: The quiet officer is astonished, and goes on the programme. For nine months the work that officer used to do lands on your desk. Your nominee will rise faster than you, and won't forget who made the nomination.

title: Oil at East Coast
body: At 4:10am on a Saturday, a tanker is holed off the Southern Islands, and by Monday there's oil on the beach at East Coast. Four agencies have formed a task force, and the Minister faces the press at 6pm with nothing written yet. It isn't your division's crisis, but whoever helps will be remembered.

choices.text: Take the pen: write the 6pm statement.
choices.outcome: Eleven drafts. At 6pm the Minister reads the ninth almost word for word, down to the metres of boom laid. On Tuesday the transcript goes round the ministries with one line added: who wrote it.

choices.text: Take the ops room: booms, beaches, rosters.
choices.outcome: Nine days of booms, shovels, contractors and volunteers who bring their own buckets. The oil gets no further than East Coast. Nobody outside the room ever learns how close it came, or who was running it.

choices.text: Stay at your own desk. It isn't your division.
choices.outcome: It wasn't your division. When the task force stands down, its thank-you lunch has forty-one names on the list, and you know every one of them. None of them is yours.

variants.title: The Siren
variants.body: At 4:10am on a Saturday, every Public Warning System siren on the island sounds the Important Message signal, and no message follows. By Monday three ministries have a task force, and there's a 6pm press conference to explain that nothing happened. It isn't your division's job, but somebody has to write the statement.

choices.text: Take the pen: explain, at 6pm, that nothing happened.
choices.outcome: Nine drafts on how to say that nothing happened without sounding as if something did. The last is read out at 6pm, and calms an island. On Tuesday three Permanent Secretaries ask who wrote it.

choices.text: Take the ops room: the hotline, the vendor, every siren.
choices.outcome: Nine days on the hotline and with the vendor, then every siren on the island checked by hand. None sounds out of turn again. That was the job, and it leaves no trace anyone upstairs will see.

choices.text: Go back to bed. It isn't your division.
choices.outcome: It wasn't your division. By Wednesday everyone on your floor can explain the Important Message signal, and does, at length. You were awake at 4:10am too. Nobody counts that.

variants.title: Lights Out
variants.body: At 7:40pm on a Thursday, a substation fault blacks out a third of the island for forty minutes, stopping lifts and trains where they stand. By morning three ministries have a task force, and the Minister has to explain it at 6pm. It isn't your division's job, but the task force is short of hands.

choices.text: Take the pen: the 6pm statement, and the apology in it.
choices.outcome: Eleven drafts, the last four about a single word: "regret". The Minister keeps it. On Friday the Head of Civil Service asks who chose the word, is told "{player.full}", and writes it down.

choices.text: Take the ops room: lifts first, then everything else.
choices.outcome: You run the room through the night: two hundred lift rescues, every one logged, none of them late. By morning the grid is back and the log is in order. Nobody reads the log.

choices.text: Go home, by the stairs. It isn't your division.
choices.outcome: It wasn't your division. You were, however, stuck in a lift at 7:40pm for thirty-one minutes, and you're the only person in the building who never mentions it.

title: The Forum Page
body: A member of the public has written to the Forum page, the letters page of the Straits Times, about a scheme your division runs. His letter is 340 words long, very angry, and right about every fact. Drafting the ministry's reply is your job, due to {senior} by Friday, and the paper will print whatever goes out.

choices.text: Draft the standard reply: thank him for his feedback.
choices.outcome: Your reply says the scheme "is regularly reviewed", in 310 words that commit to nothing. It's approved in a single round, which tells you exactly what gets approved easily here.

choices.text: Draft a reply that admits he's right, and says what will change.
choices.outcome: It goes through nine rounds of approval and comes out shorter, but the admission survives. He writes in again, to thank you. That letter doesn't get published.

choices.text: Look him up in the ministry's records first.
choices.outcome: His record gives you his address in Ang Mo Kio and the school he taught at for thirty years. You close it without doing anything with it. But you did open it, and the system logs who opens what.

title: The Posting
body: You're offered a three-year posting overseas: Washington, Beijing or Brussels. Postings like this are how officers get the experience the top jobs ask for. Your mother is eighty, lives alone in Toa Payoh, and has had lunch with you every Sunday for ten years.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Three good years. You come back with a network, a much clearer sense of how small the country is, and a mother who has learnt to video call and now rather prefers it.

choices.text: Turn it down.
choices.outcome: You give "family reasons". They're accepted at once, warmly, with complete understanding, and written into your file, where the next posting committee will read them.

choices.text: Ask for it to be deferred two years.
choices.outcome: It's deferred. It's never offered again. Nobody tells you it won't be; you simply notice, eventually, that it hasn't been.

title: The Tender
body: You chair the panel choosing a vendor for a $4 million contract, and the two bids are 0.3 points apart. The better one comes from a firm run by someone who left your ministry eighteen months ago and still sends you a Chinese New Year card. This year's arrived the week the tender closed. Contracts like this get audited.

choices.text: Award it. The bid really is better.
choices.outcome: It really is better, and you write four pages saying why, three more than anyone writes for a stranger. The card goes in the file too. Files are kept, and one day someone will read this one.

choices.text: Recuse yourself from the evaluation.
choices.outcome: You declare the card and step off the panel, with a one-page memo saying why. The panel picks the same firm without you, and running the project goes to a colleague instead of you. Your memo is the best thing in the file.

choices.text: Award it to the other vendor to be safe.
choices.outcome: The other vendor wins, on a score you had to adjust twice. The project runs eleven months late. You were right to worry about how it looked, and wrong to let that decide it.

title: Meet-the-People Session
body: An old school friend volunteers at her MP's Meet-the-People Session: every Tuesday night, residents bring their problems to their Member of Parliament, and volunteers write their appeal letters to agencies. She asks you to help. Most of the cases were decided correctly the first time. The sessions are run by the party's branch in the ward, and civil servants are meant to stay out of politics. She says lots of people help in their own time.

choices.text: Go every Tuesday for a year, in your own time.
choices.outcome: Fifty-one Tuesdays, in your own T-shirt, never the branch one. You learn more about how policy lands than in all your years of writing it. One appeal you argue properly, for a woman everyone said was hopeless, wins. The MP notices.

choices.text: Go a few times, enough to be seen.
choices.outcome: You go four times, and make sure the MP sees you on two of them. You learn very little about how policy lands. The branch learns that you are interested.

choices.text: Decline. You are a civil servant, and mean to stay neutral.
choices.outcome: Your friend says she completely understands. The branch secretary, standing next to her, also understands, and will remember your name if it ever comes up.

title: The Officer You Are Supervising
body: You're supervising a scholar, one of the high-flyers the government paid to study overseas: twenty-six, very clever, and likely to outrank you within four years. The scholar has asked you to look over a first big paper before it goes upstairs. It isn't good. Whatever you say now will be remembered when the scholar is the one above you.

choices.text: Say so plainly, and teach the scholar why.
choices.outcome: You say it isn't good, and spend an afternoon showing why. The scholar takes it well, rewrites it twice, and gets rather good. The scholar will outrank you soon, and will remember that afternoon.

choices.text: Clear it. Let the scholar find out the hard way.
choices.outcome: The paper goes up, and goes badly. Three months later the scholar is moved to a better posting anyway, which teaches a different lesson from the one you meant.

choices.text: Rewrite it yourself overnight.
choices.outcome: By morning it's a good paper with the scholar's name on it, and you're thanked for it. The scholar never learns to write, and it turns out never needs to.

title: The Leak
body: Details of a policy that hasn't been announced have appeared, accurately, on a Telegram channel. Only eleven people were sent the paper, and you're one of them. There will be an internal inquiry into all eleven, and leaking a confidential paper is the kind of thing that ends careers.

choices.text: Cooperate fully with the internal inquiry.
choices.outcome: The inquiry takes four months and concludes that the source "could not be determined". The eleven of you are never quite at ease with each other again.

choices.text: Quietly work out who it was. Tell no one.
choices.outcome: It takes a fortnight. It was {peer}, for a reason you find you have some sympathy with. You tell nobody, and {peer} never learns that you know.

choices.text: The leak was yours. Say nothing to the inquiry.
choices.outcome: You leaked it, for what you still believe were good reasons, and you sit through the inquiry saying nothing. It doesn't find you. You'll spend years finding out whether that holds.

title: The Pingat
body: This year's National Day Awards, the honours the state gives out every August, include you: a Pingat, the entry-level medal, for the scheme your division delivered. You led it, so your name went on the nomination. Your team, who did most of the work, are not on the list. Your family is already practising how to say "Pingat".

choices.text: Accept, and bring your family to the investiture.
choices.outcome: Your family dresses as if for a wedding and photographs everything, including the carpet. You realise afterwards that it was the best day they have had in years, and it cost you nothing.

choices.text: Accept, and ask that your team be recognised too.
choices.outcome: You are told this year's list is fixed. So at the division meeting you give your team the credit, by name. A mention is not a medal, and everyone knows it, but it still lands.

title: Lo Hei
body: It's the division's Chinese New Year lunch, and the Permanent Secretary is at your table. After eleven minutes of lo hei, tossing the yusheng salad as high as chopsticks allow and shouting wishes for abundance, the Permanent Secretary turns to you and asks, properly: "So, {player.given}, if your division had to stop one thing this year, what should it be?" The first project that comes to mind is your own.

choices.text: Your own project. Say why.
choices.outcome: You have about ninety seconds, and you spend all of them on why your own work should stop. The Permanent Secretary stops eating to listen, and at the end says, "Say that again on Thursday, to the committee." The people who decide promotions will be in that room.

choices.text: Another division's project. Say why.
choices.outcome: It's a reasonable answer, well argued, and the Permanent Secretary nods. The other division's project is reviewed in March. Its director never finds out who suggested it, and you never ask whether yours would have been next.

choices.text: Say that everything the division does matters.
choices.outcome: "Mm," says the Permanent Secretary, and turns to the person on the other side. That's the end of it, and you both know it.

title: The Inter-Ministry Committee
body: You're the secretariat for an Inter-Ministry Committee: you write its papers and its minutes. It has met eleven times to settle a question three ministries disagree on, and its interim finding is that "further study is warranted". No ministry wants to be the one that gave way, and {journalist} has started asking you why.

choices.text: Write a paper that forces a decision.
choices.outcome: Your paper, with your name in the footer, sets out three options and recommends one. Two ministries object to being cornered, and say so to your superiors. A decision is made anyway, mostly to stop the paper circulating.

choices.text: Keep taking excellent minutes.
choices.outcome: Your minutes are widely admired. The committee meets fourteen more times. At the end you're commended "for your support of the committee's work", and the question is still open.

choices.text: Tell {journalist} about the deadlock.
choices.outcome: {journalist}'s story runs that weekend, and a decision follows within a month. You were right about what needed to happen. The service remembers, for much longer, that you made it happen through the press.

title: The Ballot
body: You've applied for a new flat from HDB, the government's housing board, for the fourth time: a four-room BTO, built to order, in a non-mature estate far from the centre. Flats go by ballot, and every ballot you lose is another year of waiting. At work you are, technically, the government, and a friend from school now works at HDB.

choices.text: Ballot again like everyone else.
choices.outcome: Queue number 2,847, for 610 flats. You laugh in the lift. At the next family dinner you explain the scheme much better than before, because now you've also lost.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB whether anything is coming up.
choices.outcome: Nothing your friend tells you is secret; it's all on the HDB website three weeks later. Three weeks early is the whole favour, and you both know its exact size. You apply for the launch your friend mentioned, and get a flat.

choices.text: Buy a resale flat, second-hand. Take the loan.
choices.outcome: Done by Thursday. The cash you pay above the valuation hurts for eleven years, and you never again have to explain a queue number at a family dinner.

variants.title: The Prime Launch
variants.body: You're applying for a new flat from HDB, the government's housing board, in a Prime project: central and cheaper now, but you'd have to live there ten years and repay part of the subsidy when you sell. Thousands have applied, and the queue is already longer than the estate. A friend from school now works at HDB.

choices.text: Apply, and take your chances.
choices.outcome: Queue number 1,206, for 290 flats. You do the arithmetic once, and then decide not to do it again.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB how the next launch looks.
choices.outcome: Your friend tells you which launch next quarter will have the shortest queue. It's on the website three weeks later, word for word. For three weeks you were the website, and you get your flat.

choices.text: Buy a second-hand resale flat instead, and stop thinking about it.
choices.outcome: You buy a 1990s five-room with its original kitchen cabinets and a view of a multi-storey carpark. The loan is long. The cabinets turn out to be very good.

variants.title: The Fifth Ballot
variants.body: You've applied for a new flat from HDB, the government's housing board, five times now and lost every ballot. The results page remembers your login. Your queue numbers, added together, would house a small town. Each lost ballot is another year of rent, and a friend from school now works at HDB.

choices.text: Ballot again.
choices.outcome: Queue number 3,104. You screenshot it for a group chat that has become, over five years, mostly a support group.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB what is coming up.
choices.outcome: Your friend walks you through next quarter's launches over kopi, and every word is on the website three weeks later. You apply for the quietest launch, and your sixth application succeeds. All you got early was public information, and a kopi.

choices.text: Buy a resale flat, second-hand. Take the loan.
choices.outcome: Done in a week. The valuation comes in below the price, and the difference must be paid in cash. That's the rule, and it's also most of your savings.

title: Committee of Supply
body: It's Committee of Supply season, when each Minister defends the ministry's budget in Parliament. The Minister has eight minutes and wants one new thing to announce from your division. Your division has nothing ready, and nobody in the meeting wants to be the one who says so.

choices.text: Offer the pilot you've been quietly building.
choices.outcome: It's eighteen months from ready, and it's announced as if it were four. You spend the next eighteen months making the announcement true after the fact, and you mostly manage it.

choices.text: Rebrand an existing scheme with a new name and a higher number.
choices.outcome: The old scheme is announced as the "Enhanced" scheme, with a bigger number in front of it. The coverage is kind. Nothing is gained, nobody is harmed, and you suspect that's most of what happens here.

choices.text: Tell the Minister there is nothing, and say so early.
choices.outcome: The Minister is annoyed for a day and grateful for a year, because the alternative was being annoyed in Parliament. Your division announces nothing, and the Minister remembers both the day and the year.

variants.title: Paragraph 14
variants.body: The Minister's budget speech for the Committee of Supply has a gap at paragraph 14, marked [ANNOUNCEMENT: DIVISION TO PROVIDE]. Your division is the division. The draft goes to the Minister on Friday, and there's nothing new to put in it.

choices.text: Fill paragraph 14 with the pilot you've been building.
choices.outcome: Paragraph 14 promises the pilot "from next year". It needs two. You spend both making paragraph 14 true, and in the end the printed record of the speech is right, a little late.

choices.text: Fill it with an old scheme, renamed and Enhanced.
choices.outcome: Paragraph 14 introduces the Enhanced scheme: the old one, with a larger number in front of it. It reads well. Nothing changes, and it's reported as a change.

choices.text: Send paragraph 14 back empty, with a note saying why.
choices.outcome: The Minister reads the note on Friday, is irritated all weekend, and on Monday cuts paragraph 14. The speech runs a minute shorter, and the Minister remembers whose minute it was.

variants.title: The Rehearsal
variants.body: A week before the Committee of Supply debate, the Minister rehearses the budget speech aloud in the boardroom while the press secretary times it. At your division's page the Minister stops, reads it twice, and asks the room what, exactly, is new. Everyone looks at you.

choices.text: Answer with the pilot, though it isn't ready.
choices.outcome: You describe the pilot as rather further along than it is. The Minister likes it, and it's in the speech by evening. The next two years are spent catching up with that evening.

choices.text: Answer with an old scheme, newly Enhanced.
choices.outcome: "An Enhanced scheme, Minister." The press secretary writes it down. The coverage is warm and calls it new. Apart from its name, nothing about it is.

choices.text: Answer that nothing is new, and nothing should be dressed up as new.
choices.outcome: The room goes very still. The Minister finishes the rehearsal without your page, thanks everyone, and leaves without looking at you. On the day, the speech runs seven minutes, not eight.

title: The Reorganisation
body: Your division is being moved to another ministry. The new org chart has one fewer director-level box than the old one, and the two people in line for the good box are you and {peer}. Your nine officers need new postings too, and HR will settle whichever case is pushed first.

choices.text: Fight for your people's postings first.
choices.outcome: You place all nine of your officers before you place yourself, and {peer} gets the good box. The nine know exactly what you did, and the sharpest of them, a young assistant director, will one day be in a position to repay it.

choices.text: Secure the good box for yourself first.
choices.outcome: You get the box, a week before {peer} would have. Your nine are placed adequately, and the division's manner towards you changes in a way nobody ever says out loud. {peer} congratulates you in writing.

choices.text: Volunteer to run the transition.
choices.outcome: Nine months of thankless plumbing: files, systems, seating plans. It goes unusually smoothly, so nobody notices, except the two people whose opinion of you decides your next five years.

title: The Engagement Exercise
body: You're writing the report on a national conversation: forty sessions, eleven hundred citizens, and a launch already booked. The report was designed around three pillars the Minister announced in advance. The feedback is overwhelmingly about the cost of living, and it fits none of them.

choices.text: Add a fourth pillar.
choices.outcome: The design is spoiled and the report is true. It's published with the fourth pillar looking slightly bolted on, because it was, because it had to be.

choices.text: Distribute the feedback across the three existing pillars.
choices.outcome: It fits beautifully, and the launch goes well. Somewhere in a file is the spreadsheet of what eleven hundred people actually said. It isn't the report, and you're the only one who has read both.

choices.text: Publish the raw feedback alongside the report.
choices.outcome: Nobody has done it before. After a fortnight of nervous meetings at three levels, it's allowed. It becomes the most-read government document of the year, and the people who had to approve it don't thank you for the fortnight.

title: The New Reporting Officer
body: {senior}, your reporting officer until now, has been given more to run, so you now report to someone new from another ministry, who knows nothing about you and has brought two trusted people along. The newcomer will write your appraisals. Meanwhile the division's hardest file, a review the Permanent Secretary wants by December, has nobody on it.

choices.text: Make yourself indispensable on the hardest file.
choices.outcome: The review takes eight months, and goes in before December. Your new reporting officer rates people strictly on what they've done, which turns out to be rarer than you'd thought, and suits you well.

choices.text: Be useful to the newcomer's two people.
choices.outcome: You become the person they ask where things are and whom to see. It's a real position and a small one, and you hold it for as long as they stay.

choices.text: Keep your head down until the newcomer leaves.
choices.outcome: The newcomer is in no hurry to leave. Meanwhile your appraisals go flat, and every promotion board for the rest of your career will see the line.

variants.title: Standing Up
variants.body: Your new reporting officer starts on Monday, and {senior}, who had the job until now, has moved up a floor to run something bigger. The newcomer spent twenty-two years in the army, holds the morning meeting standing up, and has brought two officers from the old unit. Nobody has briefed the newcomer on the year's most urgent file: the legal opinion that a decision due in March rests on.

choices.text: Brief the newcomer on the legal opinion yourself.
choices.outcome: You brief your new reporting officer on the legal opinion in nine minutes, standing, and the March decision goes through. From then on you're asked for by surname, which in the newcomer's vocabulary is a commendation.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to the newcomer's two officers.
choices.outcome: They know the newcomer; you know the building. By Christmas you're the fourth chair at their lunch table, and you keep it. It's the chair by the window.

choices.text: Do as you're told, and wait for the newcomer to move on.
choices.outcome: The newcomer shows no sign of moving on. Your appraisals start to read like a roll call: present, correct, in line, and visible to every promotion board after.

variants.title: The Deck
variants.body: {senior}, your reporting officer until now, is too busy to supervise you, so you're getting a new one: a mid-career hire from a consulting firm who wants everything as a deck, and has brought two former colleagues in on contract. This year's biggest decision rests on a file that won't fit on a slide: an Act, two amendments and a court case.

choices.text: Take the file that won't fit on a slide.
choices.outcome: You walk your new reporting officer through the Act, the amendments and the court case in an afternoon. The newcomer is quick, and from then on rates you on what you know.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to the two consultants.
choices.outcome: They need someone who knows how a paper really moves through the building, and you do. They bill for it. Their final report thanks you in a footnote, as "a key stakeholder".

choices.text: Wait for the new boss to go back to the private sector.
choices.outcome: Your new boss likes it here, and stays. Your appraisals stop changing by so much as a word, and every promotion board after reads the identical years as one.

harder.title: The New Reporting Officer
harder.body: {senior}, your reporting officer until now, has been given more to run, and someone new from another ministry will write your appraisals. Since your first months you've gone for the hard work first, and the division's hardest file has nobody on it. What the newcomer sees this year is what your file will say about you for years.

choices.text: Take the hardest file, as you always have.
choices.outcome: The review goes in before December. Your new reporting officer rates people on what they've done, and you've done a great deal. It suits you, and it's become what people expect of you.

choices.text: This time, start with the newcomer's two people.
choices.outcome: You learn their names before you learn the newcomer's habits. By March they ask you where things are and whom to see. The hardest file goes to someone else, who is tired by December.

choices.text: Let someone else take the file. Keep your head down.
choices.outcome: Someone else takes the hard file, and you do your own work, quietly. The newcomer forms a view of you anyway, and the view is "steady", which every promotion board after will read.

network.title: The New Reporting Officer
network.body: {senior}, your reporting officer until now, has been given more to run, and someone new from another ministry will write your appraisals, with two trusted people in tow. Since your first months you've made a point of knowing who matters. What the newcomer sees this year is what your file will say about you for years.

choices.text: Leave the networking. Take the hardest file.
choices.outcome: You take the file nobody wanted, and finish it in eight months. Fewer people know your face this year. Your new reporting officer knows your work, which turns out to be the one that counts.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to the newcomer's two people.
choices.outcome: By Christmas you're the fourth chair at their lunch table. It's a real position and a small one, and you hold it for as long as they stay.

choices.text: Step back, and keep your head down.
choices.outcome: You stop going to the lunches and do your own work. The newcomer barely knows your name by June, and the two trusted people have found someone else to ask.

head_down.title: The New Reporting Officer
head_down.body: {senior}, your reporting officer until now, has been given more to run, and someone new from another ministry will write your appraisals. Since your first months you've kept your head down and done what's in front of you, well and without fuss. What the newcomer sees this year is what your file will say about you for years.

choices.text: This time, ask for the hardest file.
choices.outcome: You ask for the file nobody wanted, and the newcomer, who doesn't know you're usually quiet, hands it over without surprise. It goes in before December. You're slightly surprised you asked.

choices.text: This time, get to know the newcomer's people.
choices.outcome: You start having lunch with the newcomer's two people. They're friendly, and by March they're asking you where things are. You find you're good at this.

choices.text: Keep your head down, as you always have.
choices.outcome: You do your own work well, and the newcomer notices it the way you notice a clock that keeps time. Your appraisals go flat, and every promotion board after will read the same line.

title: The Secondment
body: You're offered a two-year secondment to a statutory board in trouble: one of the agencies the ministry runs at arm's length, whose accounts have had to be corrected three years running. It isn't a promotion. A posting like this is either a proving ground, where careers are made, or a siding, where they're parked, and nobody will tell you which.

choices.text: Go, and fix it.
choices.outcome: You go, and spend the first year just finding out what's wrong with the accounts. The board's next annual report will tell everyone whether you fixed it, and which kind of posting this was.

choices.text: Go, and keep your head down for two years.
choices.outcome: You go, do what's asked and nothing more, and the board stays in trouble. That's how a posting becomes a siding. Nobody parks you there; you park yourself.

choices.text: Refuse it and stay where you are visible.
choices.outcome: You stay where people can see you, doing work that doesn't much matter. Being seen doing that turns out to count for less than a hard job nobody was watching.

title: The Adviser Suggests Something
body: After a community event in your neighbourhood, the grassroots adviser, the party's Member of Parliament who oversees the area's community groups, stops you at the lift lobby to say you handle yourself well with people. The adviser says it to nobody else that evening. Everyone knows what this is: the first, deniable step in finding people the party might one day field at an election. Whatever you say back will be passed on.

choices.text: Say you have thought about it.
choices.outcome: You have not said yes to anything. You have said the one sentence that puts your name on the party's list of people to watch, and the adviser will be in touch.

choices.text: Laugh it off.
choices.outcome: The adviser laughs too, and the subject closes. The adviser never raises it again, and for a long time nobody else from the party does either.

title: The Figure, Again

options.text: the part where {senior} asked you to
the part where you were asked to

body: Years ago, when your scheme's usage came in at 31%, you put it on a slide as "30-60%". Now the Auditor-General's Office is auditing the scheme and has asked for the original figure for that year. The request is routine and addressed to {player.full}, and the auditors will compare it with the slide.

choices.text: Send the real figure, and explain the slide.
choices.outcome: You write it all down plainly, including {asked}. The auditors accept it with a coolness that lasts about two years and then, oddly, turns into a kind of respect.

choices.text: Send the range, and say the raw file wasn't kept.
choices.outcome: The raw file was kept. It's kept in three places, and the auditors find two of them. Telling an auditor something untrue in writing is much worse than a wide range on a slide, and you've now done it.

title: Questions About the Tender
body: Some years back you awarded a $4 million contract to a firm run by a former colleague, the one whose Chinese New Year card arrived the week the tender closed. Now a Member of Parliament has filed a parliamentary question about contracts won by firms run by former civil servants. The answer will list fourteen contracts in an annex, and yours is one of them.

choices.text: Let your four pages of reasons speak for you.
choices.outcome: Your four pages are meticulous. The question is answered in eleven lines, and nobody ever discusses the annex. The care you took at the time was the whole defence, and you took it because you knew you'd need it.

choices.text: Ask a friend drafting the answer to leave yours out.
choices.outcome: Your contract quietly drops out of the annex. Your friend now knows something about you that nobody else does, and anyone who checks the full list of contracts will find one missing.

title: A Journalist Has Been Asking

options.text: Years ago, as the secretariat of an Inter-Ministry Committee, you told {journalist} about its deadlock, which you weren't supposed to discuss. Now {journalist.formal} rings, without naming anyone, to warn you that a reporter at another paper is rebuilding that old story from everyone who was on the circulation list. The reporter has your number.

Something confidential got out once, years ago, and you were the one who let it out. Now {journalist} is piecing the old story back together, calling everyone who was on the circulation list at the time. Today {journalist.formal} called you.

Something confidential got out once, years ago, and you were the one who let it out. Now a reporter is piecing the old story back together from everyone who was on the circulation list at the time, and has just called you.

body: {caller}

choices.text: Decline to comment. Say nothing to anyone.
choices.outcome: The story runs without you in it, this time. You spend a fortnight finding out how much of your calm depended on nobody ever asking.

choices.text: Tell the most senior person you answer to, before the reporter does.
choices.outcome: It's the worst forty minutes of your career, and it ends the matter for good. You're thanked for coming forward, and it's meant. It's also never forgotten.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: Over a decade ago, you put forward the quiet officer who did your division's real work for the leadership programme, instead of yourself. That officer is a Deputy Secretary now, and has been asked to suggest names for another Deputy Secretary post: the last rung below Permanent Secretary.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let your old nominee decide.
choices.outcome: Your name goes in. Neither of you mentions the nomination from years ago. It was never a transaction, and it stays that way by not being mentioned.

choices.text: Say first that your old nominee owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: Your old nominee says that is understood, and puts your name in anyway. That's how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: Over a decade ago, you nominated the quiet officer who did your division's real work for the leadership programme, instead of yourself. That officer has since overtaken you, is now a Deputy Secretary with a post to fill, and asks for you by name.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Neither of you mentions the nomination. You're given the hardest file in the division, and everything you write is read twice.

choices.text: Say first that your old nominee owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: Your old nominee says that is understood, and asks for you anyway. That's how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: Over a decade ago, you nominated the quiet officer who did your division's real work for the leadership programme, instead of yourself. That officer is a Permanent Secretary now, younger than you and faster, and has been asked for names for another Permanent Secretary post, the last rung there is. You're a Deputy Secretary.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let your old nominee decide.
choices.outcome: Your name goes in. Neither of you mentions the nomination from years ago, because the whole point of it was that it was never a transaction.

choices.text: Say first that your old nominee owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: Your old nominee says that is understood, and puts your name in anyway. That's how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: Over a decade ago, you nominated the quiet officer who did your division's real work for the leadership programme, instead of yourself. That officer is a Permanent Secretary now too, and you sit on the same committees. Your old nominee has been asked, quietly, which fellow Permanent Secretaries the party should one day invite to tea: its first quiet approach to someone it might ask to stand for Parliament.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let your old nominee answer.
choices.outcome: One name is given. You only find out whose from the way certain people start greeting you in lifts.

choices.text: Say first that your old nominee owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: Your old nominee says that is understood, and gives your name anyway. That's how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: Over a decade ago, you put forward the quiet officer who did your old division's real work for the leadership programme, instead of yourself. That officer is a Permanent Secretary now. From time to time the Prime Minister's office asks Permanent Secretaries for a frank view of the politicians they work with, before deciding who goes up. Your old nominee has been asked about you.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let your old nominee answer.
choices.outcome: The view goes in, and you never see it. At the next reshuffle the commentary calls you someone the civil service rates. That is the one review a politician never gets to read, and it helps.

choices.text: Say first that your old nominee owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: Your old nominee says that is understood, and gives an honest view anyway, which is how you finally learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: The young scholar you once supervised is your Deputy Secretary now. Back then you said plainly that the scholar's first big paper wasn't good, and spent an afternoon showing why. After a routine meeting your Deputy Secretary stays behind and says, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Say it was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: Your Deputy Secretary has put your name forward for something, you learn, on the strength of one afternoon years ago. You go back to your desk and sit there for a while.

choices.text: Say the paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: Your Deputy Secretary laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. It is, apparently, the only feedback ever worth keeping.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: The young scholar you once supervised is a Deputy Secretary now, like you, at an age you won't ask about. Back then you said plainly that the scholar's first big paper wasn't good. After a joint meeting the scholar stays behind and says, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Say it was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: The scholar has put your name forward for something, you learn, on the strength of one afternoon years ago. You go back to your office and sit there for a while.

choices.text: Say the paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: The scholar laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. It is, apparently, the only feedback ever worth keeping.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: The young scholar you once supervised is now one of your Deputy Secretaries. Back then you said plainly that the scholar's first big paper wasn't good. After a routine meeting your Deputy Secretary stays behind and says, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Say it was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: Your Deputy Secretary now tells new officers the same things, in the same words, and reports that they dislike it just as much. It's said as though this were the point. It was.

choices.text: Say the paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: Your Deputy Secretary laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. It is, apparently, the only feedback ever worth keeping.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: The young scholar you once supervised is a Permanent Secretary now. Back then you said plainly that the scholar's first big paper wasn't good, and spent an afternoon showing why. After briefing a group of MPs on a bill, your old scholar waits until the room has emptied and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Say it was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: The favour is returned: from now on, the scholar you once taught tells you when your speeches are bad. It happens often. They get better, and the newspapers notice before the party does.

choices.text: Say the paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: A laugh, and the reply that this is why your briefs are now written by a Permanent Secretary personally. They are very good. They are also eleven pages long, and you are expected to read all of them.

title: An Invitation to Tea
body: An email invites you to tea. The sender's title is not explained and there is no agenda, but everyone in the service knows what this is: the governing party is sounding you out to stand for Parliament, as one of its candidates at the next general election. Go, and your whole career will be looked at. Decline, and you stay a civil servant, and the invitation never comes again.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: Tea is served, and the conversation is about nothing for forty minutes. Then a second guest arrives with a folder: everything in your career that could embarrass the party. The newcomer opens it, and reads.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You write three sentences and delete two of them. The reply thanks you for your candour. Others invited that year say yes. You will not be asked again, and you will think about this for the rest of your life.

variants.body: A phone call: a warm, unhurried voice, which gives no surname, asks if you are free for tea on Thursday. You are suddenly very free. This is how the governing party sounds out people it might ask to stand for Parliament, as its candidates at the next general election. Go, and they will look closely at your past. Say no, and nobody calls again.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: Tea is at a club with carpet so thick it swallows footsteps, and the talk is about nothing for an hour. Then the second pot comes, and so does a second visitor, with a folder on your career. The visitor opens it, and reads.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You say you are honoured, but committed to the service. The voice understands completely, and moves on to the next name on its list. Others invited that year say yes, and you never hear the voice again.

variants.body: A hand-delivered envelope on your desk asks whether you might spare an hour for tea and a conversation "about the future". It does not say who sent it. It does not need to: this is the governing party's first approach to someone it may ask to stand at the next election, as one of its candidates. Accept, and the party will go through your whole career for anything that could embarrass it. Decline, and the future goes ahead without you.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: The hour is in a quiet room with very good chairs. Two people ask for your views on the country. Then the older of the two, without any change of tone, opens a folder on your career and begins to read from it.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You reply by hand, because it seems right, and say no. A handwritten thank-you arrives within a day. Others invited that year say yes, and the future happens without you in it.

title: The Background Check
body: Before the party puts you up for election, it checks everything that could come out in a campaign. The person who read from the folder at your tea is back with it, now as your interviewer. Whatever you admit counts against you; admit too much and the invitation quietly lapses. Whatever you hide may surface during the campaign. Nobody says which parts of the folder are the worry.

choices.text: Disclose everything, including the things they may not have.
choices.outcome: Your interviewer listens without writing anything until you have finished, then writes for a long time. Whatever happens next, nothing in that folder can surprise you on the campaign trail.

choices.text: Answer exactly what is asked and nothing more.
choices.outcome: The questions are precise and so are your answers. Your interviewer thanks you. Nobody mentions the folder again. It is still there, and anything in it can still come out.

variants.body: The background check, in a room with a window that does not open. Before fielding you, the party must know what could come out in a campaign. The person who read from the folder at your tea asks the questions; a colleague writes. Your folder lies between them, closed. Somehow that is worse. Admit too much and the invitation lapses. Hide something and it may surface later.

choices.text: Tell them everything, including what is not in the folder.
choices.outcome: You talk for forty minutes and the colleague fills four pages. At the end your questioner says, "Thank you, {player.formal}. That was very complete." It sounds like the highest praise either of them is allowed to give.

choices.text: Answer the questions you are asked, and only those.
choices.outcome: Precise questions, precise answers, and nobody opens the folder. When you leave it is still on the table, closed. It will be opened again later, somewhere else, perhaps by a journalist.

variants.body: The party's background check starts as a form: forty-two questions, three about companies you have never heard of and one, question thirty-one, about a company you have. Then a meeting with the person who read from the folder at your tea, to "go through it together". What you admit now costs you, and too much ends the invitation. What you leave out may come out in the campaign.

choices.text: Go through all of it, including question thirty-one.
choices.outcome: You go through everything, and then the things the form did not ask. The meeting runs an hour over. Nobody seems to mind; that appears to have been the point.

choices.text: Go through what is on the form.
choices.outcome: Every question is answered completely and exactly. Question thirty-one is answered in eleven words. The meeting ends on time, and the folder goes back into a drawer you do not get to see.

title: The General Election
body: The party is fielding you at the general election, in a GRC: a large ward split into divisions, where you run as one of a team of five and voters elect the whole team together. You have resigned from the service to stand, and if you lose, the service will not take you back. The minister leading your team asks which division you will look after.

choices.text: Take the division you're given: share the risk, and the credit.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts, meeting voters at every market and coffee shop, with your name fourth on the poster. You shake eleven thousand hands and understand, with total clarity, that almost none of this is about you.

choices.text: Take the division the opposition is fighting for.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts in the four blocks the opposition has decided to win, while your teammates take the friendlier ones. The minister leading your team calls every evening to ask how it is going, and listens to the answer.

choices.text: Ask for a single seat of your own instead, alone against one opponent: all the risk, and all the credit.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts, meeting voters at every market and coffee shop, alone, against a decent opponent with volunteers on every floor. Nobody carries you, and if it goes wrong, there is nobody else to blame.

variants.body: Polling Day is announced on a Monday, and the party names you as a candidate in a GRC: a large ward, split into divisions, that elects a team of five together. You have resigned from the service to stand, so losing ends your career: the service will not take you back. Now you choose your division.

choices.text: Stand with the team, in the division you're given: shared risk, shared credit.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts, meeting voters block by block, teach you which blocks have lifts that stop on every floor. The minister leading your team does the rally speeches. You do the lifts.

choices.text: Stand with the team, in its hardest division.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts, block by block, in the division the other side has picked to fight for. Your name is fourth on the poster and first on every complaint, and the team notices which of you went where.

choices.text: Ask to stand alone in a single seat instead: your risk, your credit.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts, meeting voters block by block, against a real opponent and with nobody to share the result with. Yours is the only name on your posters. It is thrilling for exactly one day.

variants.body: The party's candidates are photographed in a school hall that smells of floor polish. You have resigned from the service to stand, and if you lose, the service will not take you back. The party has you on a GRC team of five, each looking after a division, which voters elect together. It asks which division you want.

choices.text: Take the division you're offered.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts in a team of five, through markets, coffee shops and lift lobbies, meeting voters. At every coffee shop someone asks which one you are. By the end of the campaign, you can answer.

choices.text: Take the division nobody wants.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts in the division the opposition is targeting, where residents have their questions ready before you reach the lift. Nobody on the team says thank you. Everyone on it knows.

choices.text: Ask for a single seat instead, alone against one opponent.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts, meeting voters at every market and coffee shop, as the only candidate anyone in the ward asks for. By the last rally your voice has gone and your opponent's has not. It feels significant, and is not.

title: The Maiden Speech
body: Your maiden speech, your first in Parliament, falls on day three of the debate on the President's Address, which opens each new Parliament. It tells the House, the press and the party what kind of Member you mean to be. You are a backbencher, a Member with no government job, and the Whip, who keeps the party's backbenchers voting together, will read every line. Hansard, the official record, keeps every word. You have written three drafts, and now you must choose which one to give.

choices.text: The draft about your ward.
choices.outcome: Lifts, hawkers, and the chess table at a void deck, the open ground floor under a block. Three colleagues call it lovely in the lift, and your residents cut it out of the newsletter. Theirs is the only review that votes.

choices.text: The draft about the one thing from the service you believe.
choices.outcome: It is quoted, and for once the quoted line is the one you meant: "If a form needs a helpline, the form is the problem." A Minister you have never met sends a note: "That needed saying." The Whip sends a longer note, about what government backbenchers say in public.

choices.text: The draft praising the policy you used to doubt.
choices.outcome: Fluent, generous and on message. The Minister responsible nods twice. In your old ministry, an officer who sat through your objections for years reads it in Hansard and forwards it on without comment.

variants.body: Day three of the debate on the President's Address, which opens each new Parliament: at 4:40pm you rise in the House to give your maiden speech, your first. It sets how the party and the press see you for years. You are a backbencher, a Member with no government job, and the Whip, who keeps backbenchers voting with the party, will read every line. Hansard, the official record, keeps every word. You have written three versions, all finished, and now you must choose which one to give.

choices.text: Give the version about your ward.
choices.outcome: Eleven minutes on your blocks, your hawkers and the chess table in the void deck, the open ground floor of one of them. It is warm, local and over before the break. Your ward's newsletter prints it in full.

choices.text: Give the version with the thing you believe.
choices.outcome: Eleven minutes on what you believed in the service and could never say there: "If a form needs a helpline, the form is the problem." The House goes quiet, the good kind. Afterwards the Whip's note to you is longer than that line.

choices.text: Give the version praising the policy you once doubted.
choices.outcome: Generous and on message. The Minister responsible thanks you by name in the wrap-up. Your old colleagues, who heard your doubts for years, read it in Hansard and say nothing.

variants.body: Your maiden speech, your first in the House, as Members call Parliament, is next week. You are a backbencher, a Member with no government job, and the office of the Whip, who keeps backbenchers voting with the party, has sent guidance on length and tone, and a sample first line: "I rise in support of the motion." Whatever follows it goes into Hansard, the official record, and tells the party what kind of Member you will be. You have written three drafts of what follows it, and now you must choose which one to give.

choices.text: Write the rest about your ward.
choices.outcome: The rest is about your ward, and it is good. A resident posts the Hansard link in the block's WhatsApp group with the caption "our one". You keep a screenshot.

choices.text: Write the rest about what you believe.
choices.outcome: The rest is the thing you believed in the service and never said: "If a form needs a helpline, the form is the problem." It is quoted, mostly correctly. The Whip's office sends further guidance, this time addressed to you alone.

choices.text: Write the rest in the same spirit, and keep your doubts.
choices.outcome: Nineteen minutes in support of the motion, with your doubts kept for later. The Whip's office uses your speech as next year's sample: the first line, and all the rest.

title: The Town Council
body: Lift C at Blk 77 has broken down nine times this year, and your Town Council, which runs the estates in your ward, must decide what to do. A proper replacement means a tender, which takes five months. {grassroots}, the {grassroots.title}, knows a contractor who could start on Monday if the tender is waived. Waivers are allowed in an emergency, and auditors read every one.

choices.text: Tender it properly, and explain the delay.
choices.outcome: Five months of complaints at every Tuesday session. The new lift comes in on budget from the lowest compliant bid. Years later the auditors read the file and find nothing to say.

choices.text: Waive the tender. Call {grassroots}'s contractor.
choices.outcome: The lift runs again in eleven weeks and the block is delighted. The waiver's justification is two lines long. The Town Councils Financial Rules expect more, and so, one day, will an auditor.

choices.text: Have the regular contractor patch it while the tender runs.
choices.outcome: The regular contractor patches Lift C six times in five months, at a cost the finance committee reads out slowly. The new lift arrives on budget, and the patches are minuted separately.

variants.body: Blk 77's lift keeps breaking down, and the Town Council, which runs the estates in your ward, meets to decide on a new one. The slide from the managing agent, the firm that runs the estate day to day, has three options. The third, circled in pen, comes from {grassroots}, the {grassroots.title}: a firm that could start on Monday, without a tender. Skipping a tender is allowed in an emergency, and auditors check every time it happens. Every head turns to you.

choices.text: Choose the tender, and minute why.
choices.outcome: The minutes record why, in a paragraph you dictate yourself. {grassroots} votes with you and does not speak to you at the tea break. The lift is replaced in five months.

choices.text: Choose the circled option, as an emergency.
choices.outcome: The firm starts on Monday and finishes in eleven weeks. The minutes say "emergency" twice. At the next block party you thank {grassroots} in front of the firm's banner, and the waiver waits on file for the auditors.

choices.text: Propose a fourth option: patch it, and tender.
choices.outcome: The meeting agrees, with relief, to the option you have just invented. The regular contractor keeps the lift running, mostly. The tender closes on time, and so, eventually, does the lift door.

variants.body: At 8am you are on the fourteenth floor of Blk 77, because the lift is not. A resident in a wheelchair has missed two dialysis sessions. A proper tender for a new lift takes five months. {grassroots}, the {grassroots.title}, hands you a phone: a contractor who can start on Monday, if your Town Council, which runs the estates in your ward, waives the tender and answers for it later.

choices.text: Hand the phone back. The tender stays.
choices.outcome: The Town Council helps her down the stairs, with a day's notice, for every session of the tender's five months. At the new lift's opening she tells you there are 168 steps.

choices.text: Take the call. Monday it is.
choices.outcome: The contractor starts on Monday. The lift works by Christmas and she makes every session. The paperwork follows in January, written to fit what happened. Auditors prefer it the other way round.

choices.text: Get the regular contractor out today, and tender the rest.
choices.outcome: The regular contractor has the lift moving by evening, and patches it twice more by Christmas. The tender runs its five months. She does not miss a session, and never lets you forget the morning.

title: The National Bonus
body: As a minister, you are paid a National Bonus: three months' extra salary if the country hits four targets, up to six if it beats them, nothing if it misses. The four are jobs, GDP growth, typical incomes, and the incomes of the lowest-paid fifth of workers. Your ministry has money for one of two policies: one lifts the lowest incomes, the other lifts GDP.

choices.text: Fund the policy that lifts the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: It is expensive, unglamorous and slow, and it works: the lowest incomes rise. Your bonus rises too, but no one talks about it.

choices.text: Fund the policy that lifts GDP.
choices.outcome: GDP moves first and fastest, and your bonus comes in at six months, the most it can be. There is an annex on who gained. You skip the annex.

choices.text: Ask the other ministers whether any of you should be paid on targets you can move.
choices.outcome: You ask at the ministers' weekly meeting. The room hears the question in complete silence. It is minuted, and answered at great length without being answered at all. From then on your colleagues choose their words around you.

variants.body: The Public Service Division sends you a three-page note on your pay as a minister. Page two explains the National Bonus: three months' extra salary if the country hits four targets for jobs, growth and incomes, one of them the incomes of the lowest-paid fifth of workers, up to six if it beats them, nothing if it misses. Page three lists two policies your ministry could fund: one lifts the lowest incomes, the other lifts GDP. There is money for one.

choices.text: Fund the policy for the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: It is slow, costly and unglamorous, and it works: the lowest incomes rise, and with them your bonus. Nobody, at any point, mentions page two.

choices.text: Fund the policy for GDP.
choices.outcome: Quicker and cleaner, and it moves the figure everyone watches. Your bonus comes in at six months, the most it can be. The annex on who gained is on page nine, and you stop reading at page eight.

choices.text: Ask the other ministers whether any of you should be paid on targets you can move.
choices.outcome: The question is heard in complete stillness, and minuted. It is answered at length without being answered at all. Colleagues now choose their words near you, and the minute is filed where it can be found.

variants.body: Your ministry's chief economist explains the National Bonus on a whiteboard: three months' extra salary when the country hits four targets for jobs, growth and incomes, up to six when it beats them. The explanation is brisk until it reaches the line saying the bonus is paid to ministers, including you. Then it slows down. One policy on your desk lifts the lowest incomes, another lifts GDP, and there is money for one.

choices.text: Choose the policy that lifts the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: It is expensive and slow, and in two years it works: the lowest incomes rise, and so does your bonus. The economist wipes the whiteboard, your pay included, before anyone can photograph it.

choices.text: Choose the policy that lifts headline GDP.
choices.outcome: The headline figure moves first and fastest. Your National Bonus comes in at six months, the most the formula allows. The economist's slide on who gained is moved to the appendix.

choices.text: Ask the other ministers whether this is how any of you should be paid.
choices.outcome: The ministers' weekly meeting hears the question in silence and minutes it with care. It is answered fully, and not at all. People adjust how they speak near you, and the minute stays in the file.

title: The Correction Direction
body: A post about your ministry's scheme is going viral. It is wrong in two places and, awkwardly, right in the third. Under POFMA, the law against online falsehoods, you can direct whoever posted it to attach a correction notice, fixing the two wrong points in public and saying nothing about the third. Or you can answer the post yourself, and admit the point it got right.

choices.text: Issue the correction direction.
choices.outcome: The correction notice appears. It is factually unimpeachable and fixes two of the three points. The third keeps circulating, now with a grievance attached: the government corrected everything except the part that was true.

choices.text: Answer the third point publicly instead.
choices.outcome: At 11pm you concede the point in a Facebook post, in your own words. It is shared more than anything your ministry has ever published, half the time by people who dislike you. You are now on record as having admitted it.

variants.body: A thread on HardwareZone, the online forum, about your ministry's scheme is on its fortieth page. The first post, which everyone quotes, is wrong about the eligibility age and the payout, and right about the waiting time. Under POFMA, the law against online falsehoods, you can direct the forum to pin a correction notice above it, fixing the two errors and leaving the waiting time standing. Or you can reply yourself.

choices.text: Issue the correction direction.
choices.outcome: A correction notice is pinned above the first post, fixing the age and the payout. Page forty-one is about the waiting time. Nobody corrected that, because it was right, and the thread has noticed.

choices.text: Reply in the thread, and concede the waiting time.
choices.outcome: You reply under your own name: two corrections and one concession. The thread is polite for nearly a page, then returns to the waiting time, now quoting you as the office holder who admitted it.

variants.body: A retired officer from your ministry has posted a long critique of its scheme, with three diagrams. Two are wrong. The third is right, to the decimal, redrawn from memory from an internal paper the officer once worked on. Under POFMA, the law against online falsehoods, you can direct the officer to attach a correction notice that fixes the two wrong ones and says nothing about the third.

choices.text: Issue the correction direction.
choices.outcome: The correction notice runs above the post and fixes two diagrams. The third stays up, uncorrected, and becomes the most widely shared chart your ministry has ever produced.

choices.text: Post the third diagram yourself, and admit what it shows.
choices.outcome: You post the third diagram again, with the real numbers and a sentence admitting the problem. The retired officer shares it with one word, "Better." Your officials do not share it.

title: The Reshuffle
body: A Cabinet reshuffle is coming: the Prime Minister will move ministers between ministries, and has asked to see you on Thursday to hear where you would like to go. Taking on a hard ministry and surviving it is how ministers reach the top jobs. Staying put is comfortable, and rarely leads further. {mp} has already told you it is good news, though {mp} knows no more than you do.

choices.text: Ask for the hard ministry nobody wants.
choices.outcome: Housing, health or transport: something with a queue, a waiting list and a headline every week. You are given it at once, and the speed tells you it was going to be yours anyway. Survive it, and the top jobs open up.

choices.text: Ask to stay where you are.
choices.outcome: You stay. It is pleasant and important, and nobody, including you, will ever find out whether you could have handled something harder.

variants.body: A Cabinet reshuffle, moving ministers between ministries, will be announced on Monday. On Friday the Prime Minister's principal private secretary calls: "{player.formal}, is there any preference you would like noted?" A hard ministry is where ministers are tested for the top jobs; staying is safe. The call lasts ninety seconds, and within the hour {mp} texts to ask how it went.

choices.text: Note a preference for the hardest ministry going.
choices.outcome: You name housing, health and transport. On Monday you are given one of them, announced so smoothly that the press release was plainly typed before the call. Survive it, and you will be in line for more.

choices.text: Note a preference for staying put.
choices.outcome: Your preference is noted in ninety seconds and honoured on Monday. You stay, in a ministry that runs well, as it did before you and will after you.

variants.body: A Cabinet reshuffle is due, and a newspaper's graphic puts your face in three different ministries, each with a question mark. {mp} sends you all three, with emojis. The Prime Minister's office wants twenty minutes on Thursday to hear where you would like to go. Hard ministries are how ministers rise. Staying is safe.

choices.text: Ask for whichever ministry has the longest queue.
choices.outcome: Inside the twenty minutes you are given housing, health or transport, whichever has the worst week coming. The newspaper says, for a week, that its graphic had guessed it.

choices.text: Ask to stay where you are.
choices.outcome: You stay, which the graphic had not considered. Your diary for the next five years looks very like your diary for the last five.

title: The Succession
body: The Prime Minister is stepping down, and the next generation of ministers must agree on a successor. The process is informal, which means it is decided entirely by people in a room. You are in the room, and so is the other front-runner. Put yourself forward and you may become Prime Minister. Back the other, and you get a senior portfolio but never the top job.

choices.text: Put yourself forward.
choices.outcome: You say it plainly, against convention. The room absorbs it. Nothing is decided that day, but your name is now one of the two being weighed, instead of one of the nine being listed.

choices.text: Back the other candidate. Ask for a senior portfolio.
choices.outcome: The other candidate wins, as everyone expected once you had spoken, and knows exactly who delivered it. You get everything you asked for. You will spend the rest of your career as the most powerful minister who is not Prime Minister.

title: The Work
body: {peer} is building a new scheme this year with you and three others, and it has to launch on time. It'll go out under the ministry's name, not yours: no officer's name ever goes on a government scheme. Whether anyone upstairs learns who did the work is, this once, up to you.

choices.text: Do the work well.
choices.outcome: It launches on time, and nobody says a word, because on time is what's expected. The people who write your appraisal noticed anyway.

choices.text: Do the work, and be seen doing it.
choices.outcome: You present it at the divisional meeting, with four more slides than it needed. Two people who didn't know your name now do. {peer}, who made half the slides, isn't mentioned.

choices.text: Coast. You've earned a quiet year.
choices.outcome: You leave at six every day for a year and eat dinner at a normal hour. It costs you exactly what you thought it would.

substance: A scheme goes out on time, and you're one of five people who know why.
You clear forty-one papers and write one sentence you're proud of. Nobody notices the sentence.
A memo you wrote comes back to you months later as "the ministry's position", and you let it stand.
You fix a system in March, it stops producing complaints, and nobody connects the two.
A paper you wrote goes upstairs under someone else's name, and does well there.
You catch an error in a figure three divisions had already passed, and fix it quietly.
Another ministry copies an approval process you redesigned, and doesn't credit you.
visibility: You present a scheme your team built at three forums, and by the third, people call it your scheme.
Your name is on the slide, the email and the photograph, for work that was mostly last year's.
