Someone from another ministry greets you by name in the lift. Being seen is working.
You present your team's work at a lunchtime talk, with your photo on the poster and the team in the footnotes.
A scheme you worked on gets a feature on the intranet, with a photograph of you pointing at a chart.
You sit on four panels this year, three of them about the same scheme.
A speech you didn't write mentions a scheme you worked on, and you, by name. That part you did arrange.
low: You do what's asked, on time and not a minute more, and nobody can find anything to complain about.
A quiet year at your desk. The best thing you write is your out-of-office message.
The papers come in and go out. Someone on your floor is working late, and it isn't you.
Your inbox reaches zero twice this year, which on your floor is treated as a rumour.
You attend every meeting on time and speak at none of them.
Your to-do list is shorter in December than in January, mostly by deletion.
A year of steady work, measured mostly in the emails you didn't send.

variants.body: Your job this year is a form the public fills in. It has eleven fields, and seven of them ask for things the government already knows. Removing them needs four agencies to agree, two legal opinions and a year of meetings nobody will remember. Getting it right would save a million people ten minutes each.

choices.text: Do the work properly.
choices.outcome: Three fields go. The other four turn out to be required by a regulation whose reason nobody can find. Three is a good year.

choices.text: Do the work, and make sure the right people see it.
choices.outcome: Three fields go, and your one-page note on them goes round upstairs as "a good example of citizen-centric design". You'll be asked to give the talk.

choices.text: Let the agencies sort it out among themselves.
choices.outcome: They don't. The form keeps all eleven fields. You keep your evenings, and decide that they were also a public good.

variants.body: This year you're reviewing a review: what was recommended three years ago, what was actually done, and why the gap between them is described as "phased implementation". The people who did the phasing will read your review, and some of them now outrank you.

choices.text: Write it straight.
choices.outcome: Your review says what happened. It's accepted with thanks, and its recommendations are, in due course, phased.

choices.text: Write it straight, and present it yourself.
choices.outcome: Your chart of the gap between what was promised and what was done is so clear that two directors ask for the slide. One of them later uses it against you, admiringly.

choices.text: Write it the way the last one was written.
choices.outcome: It reads beautifully and says nothing anyone could disagree with. It takes a week. You spend the rest of the year on other things, mostly lunch.

variants.body: Your ministry's hotline takes two thousand calls a week, and four hundred of them ask the same question. The website answers it, on page six. Fixing this is your job for the year, and first you have to decide whether the problem is the callers or page six.

choices.text: Fix page six.
choices.outcome: Page six becomes page one, in plain words, and calls drop by a third. The hotline team sends a cake with no message, the highest honour a hotline can give.

choices.text: Fix page six, and present the call figures.
choices.outcome: Your before-and-after chart travels further than the website ever did. Two other agencies cite it in their own papers, with your name in the footnote.

choices.text: Note it for whoever owns the website, and go home on time.
choices.outcome: Your note is clear and lands in the right inbox, where it stays. The calls continue. You're home by half past six, most days.

variants.body: A circular explaining a new rule has to reach forty agencies by the first of the month, and getting it there is your job. It's on its ninth draft. The ninth is the first one anyone outside this building could understand, and three more people still want to comment on it.

choices.text: Send the ninth draft, on time.
choices.outcome: It goes out on the twenty-eighth. Three agencies reply that it's the clearest circular they've had all year, which in agency terms is a standing ovation.

choices.text: Send it, and brief the agencies yourself.
choices.outcome: Forty agencies, four briefings, one set of slides. By the last briefing you don't need the slides, and two directors now ask for you by name.

choices.text: Leave the last draft to the next person in the chain.
choices.outcome: It goes out on the third of the month, two days late. Nobody asks why, and you were home for dinner on both days.

substance.title: The Work, Again
substance.body: {peer} is building another scheme this year, and has asked for you by name. You've made a habit of doing the work well and letting it speak for itself, while other people's names go on the slides. How you handle this one is how your working years will run after it, without anyone asking you again.

choices.text: Do it well, and let it speak, as usual.
choices.outcome: It launches on time and nobody says a word, because on time is what's expected of you now. The people who write your appraisal have stopped noticing, and started relying on it.

choices.text: Do it, and this time make sure you're seen.
choices.outcome: You present the launch yourself, with your name on the first slide, and two directors ask afterwards who you are. {peer} notices too. From now on your name goes on your work.

choices.text: Let the others carry this one. Ease off.
choices.outcome: You leave at six, and the scheme launches anyway, a week late and mostly fine. Nobody asks why. You find you don't miss the late nights as much as you'd expected.

visibility.title: The Work, Again
visibility.body: {peer} is building another scheme this year, and you're on it again. You've made a habit of being seen with your work: the slides, the forums, the photograph beside the chart. {peer} has started counting whose names are on them. How you handle this one is how your working years will run after it, without anyone asking you again.

choices.text: Do the work, and let {peer} present it.
choices.outcome: {peer} presents it well, and thanks you by name in the second minute. Fewer people upstairs know your face this year. The people who write your appraisal know your work.

choices.text: Present it, as you always do.
choices.outcome: Your slides, your forum, your photograph beside the chart. By the third presentation people call it your scheme, and {peer} has stopped volunteering to make the slides.

choices.text: Step back from it altogether this year.
choices.outcome: You hand over your slides and leave on time. The scheme launches with {peer} at the lectern. Your name stops coming up in meetings, which is restful, and then noticeable.

low.title: The Work, Again
low.body: {peer} is building another scheme this year, and needs one more person on it. You've made a habit of doing what's asked and not a minute more, and your evenings have been your own for a while. How you handle this one is how your working years will run after it, without anyone asking you again.

choices.text: Join, and do it properly this time.
choices.outcome: You join, and the late nights come back with the work. It launches on time. The people who write your appraisal notice the change before you've noticed it yourself.

choices.text: Join, and make sure upstairs sees you did.
choices.outcome: You join late and present early. Two directors who had stopped saying your name start again, and {peer}, who did most of the year's work, says nothing about it.

choices.text: Say you're stretched. Keep your evenings.
choices.outcome: {peer} finds someone else by Friday. You leave at six all year and nobody says anything, which you take as agreement. It's mostly indifference.

title: The Appraisal Conversation
body: It's your yearly appraisal conversation with {senior}: forty minutes and a form with six competency areas. What goes on the form is taken to the ranking meeting that decides your grade. Halfway through, {senior} says, "I'd like you to be more visible," without saying to whom.

choices.text: Ask directly where you stand.
choices.outcome: "Rankings aren't really something we discuss," {senior} says, kindly. It's a complete answer.

choices.text: Agree to be more visible.
choices.outcome: You volunteer for two committees. It works, in the sense that more people have now seen you.

choices.text: Ask what needs doing that nobody is doing.
choices.outcome: {senior} thinks for a moment, then names something real: a backlog nobody owns. You clear it by June. That one answer was worth the other thirty-nine minutes.

standing: At your appraisal you ask where you stand, and are told it's "not a helpful way to think about it", the most precise answer yet.
Your appraisal: forty minutes, six competency areas, and one question from you, about where you stand, that nobody writes down.
At your appraisal you ask where you stand, and are offered a coaching session on curiosity.
You ask at your appraisal where you stand, and the question is recorded under "Officer's Aspirations", a box on the form.
You ask where you stand at the end of your appraisal, when there are two minutes left.
visible: You agree again to be more visible, and at the next appraisal you're told that you have been.
Your appraisal: six competency areas, one new acronym and the phrase "stretch assignment", with you nodding at the right moments.
You're more visible this year, mostly in the background of other people's photographs.
Your visibility is praised at a meeting you went to mainly in order to be seen there.
Your visibility is discussed at your appraisal for forty minutes, in a room with no windows.
needs: At your appraisal you ask what isn't being done. By March it's done, and your name is on the list for the next good posting.
You ask what would have helped in this year's "very tight" ranking, and, unusually, you're told.
The things nobody was doing become your things, each with a thank-you for asking.
The list of work nobody is doing gets shorter by March and longer by June, with your name at the top.
You ask what needs doing. A great deal does, and now it's on your list instead of anyone else's.

variants.body: It's appraisal week. HR has redesigned the form: four areas instead of six, a new section called "Aspirations", and a box for {senior} to give an overall impression that's bigger than all the others put together. Everyone knows the big box is what decides your grade.

choices.text: Ask what your overall impression says.
choices.outcome: "It's still being calibrated." {senior} turns the form face down, gently. You'll find out with everyone else, when the grades come out.

choices.text: Fill in "Aspirations" with something ambitious.
choices.outcome: You write "to lead a cross-agency effort". A month later you're put on one, as an ordinary member. {senior} calls it a good first step.

choices.text: Ask which of the four areas actually counts.
choices.outcome: {senior} pauses, then says which area really counts: "Ownership." So you spend the year taking charge of things nobody else wanted. It shows, and it's noticed.

variants.body: This year's appraisal conversation is a video call, because {senior} is overseas on a course. The camera at the other end is off, and the connection is excellent. What's said in these forty minutes goes into this year's grade, and with the camera off you can't tell how any of it is landing.

choices.text: Ask, plainly, where you stand.
choices.outcome: "You're doing fine." There's a long silence on the line, then: "Fine is good." It's clearly not the whole sentence.

choices.text: Turn your camera on, and keep it on.
choices.outcome: Eventually the other camera comes on too. The second half of the call is noticeably warmer. You are now, in a small way, visible.

choices.text: Ask what {senior} wants done while away.
choices.outcome: {senior} lists three things. You finish two of them before {senior} flies home, and {senior} mentions it at the ranking meeting that decides grades, the only meeting that matters.

variants.body: Your appraisal conversation is in a meeting room booked for thirty minutes, and it's the only time this year {senior} will sit down with you before writing your grade. {senior} arrives twelve minutes late, from another officer's appraisal, carrying that officer's form by mistake.

choices.text: Ask, while there's time, where you stand.
choices.outcome: {senior} glances down at someone else's form and says that's above {senior.their} pay grade. It may be the only literal thing anyone says to you all year.

choices.text: Use the eighteen minutes to list what you did.
choices.outcome: You get through the list in eleven minutes. {senior} writes down four items, and they're the four taken to the ranking meeting that decides your grade. You learn which four to lead with next year.

choices.text: Ask what {senior} needs from you this year.
choices.outcome: The answer comes before {senior} has even sat down: a paper nobody has started. You start it that afternoon, and next year's appraisal begins on time.

variants.body: This year your appraisal includes anonymous feedback from the people who work around you, and {senior} reads it out. One comment says you "never say no to anything from upstairs", so the extra work lands on everyone else. Fair or not, it will go in your file.

choices.text: Ask what the comment means for your grade.
choices.outcome: {senior} says it's "a development point, not a grading point", and then that grades aren't discussed before the ranking meeting. Both halves are true, and only one of them was an answer.

choices.text: Say you'll be more visible to the people around you, not just upstairs.
choices.outcome: You start a monthly lunch for the people around you. Attendance is excellent. Next year's anonymous comment is about the lunches, and it's fond.

choices.text: Ask what {senior} needs you to say no to.
choices.outcome: {senior} names two jobs you could stop doing for upstairs. You stop both, and the people around you notice before {senior} does.

standing.title: The Appraisal Conversation
standing.body: Your yearly appraisal conversation with {senior} has come round again: forty minutes, a form, and the ranking meeting after it. Every year you ask exactly where you stand, and {senior} now has an answer ready. How you spend this one is how you'll spend every one after it.

choices.text: Ask where you stand, as you always do.
choices.outcome: {senior} gives the ready answer, word for word, and adds "as before". It's still not an answer. It has become a tradition, which is nearly the same thing.

choices.text: Agree, this time, to be more visible.
choices.outcome: You volunteer for two committees. {senior} writes "more visible" on the form, in the box where it has always said "asked about prospects".

choices.text: Ask what needs doing that nobody is doing.
choices.outcome: {senior}, braced for the usual question, is so relieved that the answer comes at once: a backlog nobody owns. You clear it by June.

visible.title: The Appraisal Conversation
visible.body: Your yearly appraisal conversation with {senior} has come round again, and the word "visible" is already on the form. Every year you agree to be more visible, and you are: committees, panels, photographs. How you spend this one is how you'll spend every one after it.

choices.text: Ask, plainly, where all that has got you.
choices.outcome: {senior} looks at the list of committees for a long time, and says it's "a strong foundation". Neither of you writes it down.

choices.text: Agree to be more visible, as usual.
choices.outcome: Two more committees and one more panel. By December you're visible in rooms you didn't know the ministry had, and the form says so, again.

choices.text: Ask what needs doing instead.
choices.outcome: {senior} names a backlog nobody owns, and you drop a committee to clear it. The committee doesn't notice you've gone. The backlog does.

needs.title: The Appraisal Conversation
needs.body: Your yearly appraisal conversation with {senior} has come round again. Every year you ask what needs doing that nobody is doing, and {senior} now arrives with a list. How you spend this one is how you'll spend every one after it.

choices.text: Ask, this time, where you stand.
choices.outcome: {senior} is surprised into honesty: "Better than you think, and not as well as you'd like." It's the most useful sentence anyone says to you all year.

choices.text: Agree, this time, to be more visible.
choices.outcome: You take the list and present it, item by item, at the divisional meeting. People who had been benefiting from your work quietly learn your name.

choices.text: Take the list, as usual.
choices.outcome: Three things nobody owned, all done by June. {senior} has started saving them up for you, which is a compliment of a kind.

title: 11:40pm, Level 9
body: It's 11:40pm, and your paper has come back for the fourth time with comments from the people who have to clear it. It's due upstairs in the morning. {junior} is still at {junior.their} desk, waiting to see what you decide. The dinner you promised to be home for was at eight.

choices.text: Finish it tonight.
choices.outcome: It's cleared at 1:20am, with {junior} proofreading the annexes. You're both thanked in one email of one word. Dinner is in the fridge, with a note that's mostly punctuation.

choices.text: Go. Send it in the morning.
choices.outcome: You send {junior} home first, and make it home yourself in time for dessert. The paper goes in at 8:40am, and the world doesn't end. You make a careful note that it didn't.

work: Working late on Level 9 becomes a habit, then a reputation.
The cleaner on your floor now says goodnight to you by name.
You miss a birthday dinner and make a deadline. By March both are forgotten, by different people.
The night guard knows your car, your floor and your usual time: late.
The lights on Level 9 go off on a timer at midnight, and you've learnt to wave at the sensor.
A deadline met at 1am is acknowledged at 9am with "Thanks, noted", all a deadline ever gets.
Your laptop battery dies at 11:58pm, mid-sentence. You take it as advice, and ignore it.
life: You leave at seven and send things in the morning, and the building doesn't fall down.
A birthday dinner, attended, while the comments on your paper wait until morning, as they always could.
You've stopped apologising for leaving on time, and two people on your floor have started doing the same.
You leave at six, the work is in by nine the next morning, and nobody can tell it wasn't written at midnight.
You leave on time, and the comments on your paper come back anyway. They're the same comments.
Dinner at eight, as promised, and your paper is none the worse for a night in the outbox.
You go home at seven again, and the midnight reply-all about your paper happens without you in it.

variants.title: Sunday, 4pm
variants.body: You're at a friend's birthday party on a Sunday afternoon when an email from upstairs asks for a brief by eight tomorrow morning. Upstairs will judge you by whether it's there at eight, not by when you wrote it. Everyone else at the table is holding cake.

choices.text: Find a quiet corner and write it now.
choices.outcome: You write it on your phone behind the cake table, and it's approved by nine. In the party photographs you're the back of a head, bent over a screen.

choices.text: Stay at the party. Write it at six tomorrow.
choices.outcome: You sing, badly, and help cut the cake. The brief goes in at 7:55am. Upstairs never asks when it was written, and that teaches you something you try to remember.

variants.title: 10:50pm, One Comment
variants.body: At 10:50pm your paper comes back from upstairs with one comment: "Can we tighten?" It's already two pages, it's due at nine tomorrow, and whoever wrote the comment is clearly still awake and waiting.

choices.text: Tighten it tonight.
choices.outcome: Two pages become one and a half. The half you cut was the only part anyone would have disagreed with, so the paper sails through.

choices.text: Reply that it's already tight, and go to bed.
choices.outcome: You reply at 10:52pm that it's already tight, and go to bed. In the morning there's a thumbs-up, which in this building counts as a concession.

work.title: Late, Again
work.body: It's late again, a paper is due upstairs in the morning, and {junior} is still at {junior.their} desk, watching what you do. These nights always end the same way: you stay and finish, whatever was planned at home. What you do tonight is what you'll do every night after it.

choices.text: Finish it tonight, as usual.
choices.outcome: Cleared at 1:10am, with {junior} on the annexes again. The thanks is one word, as before. At home the note on the fridge has stopped being punctuation and become a list.

choices.text: Go home. Send it in the morning, this once.
choices.outcome: You send {junior} home first, then go yourself. The paper goes in at 8:40am and nobody upstairs can tell. At home, the dinner is what people remember.

life.title: Late, Again
life.body: It's late again, a paper is due upstairs in the morning, and {junior} is waiting to see what you do. These nights always end the same way: you go home on time and send it in the morning, and the building hasn't fallen down yet. What you do tonight is what you'll do every night after it.

choices.text: Stay tonight, and finish it.
choices.outcome: You stay, and {junior} stays because you did. It's cleared at 1am. Upstairs says thank you, once, and the next morning {junior} looks at you as if you'd changed the rules.

choices.text: Go home, as you always do.
choices.outcome: You're home for dinner, and the paper goes in at 8:40am. Upstairs never asks when it was written. Two people on your floor now leave on time too, and say it was your idea.

title: The Budget Round
body: It's budget season, and you're bidding for what your division needs next year: eleven more officers and a new system. The ministry's total budget, you're told, won't grow at all. Every other division has been told the same, and every other bid is also for eleven of something.

choices.text: Bid big and justify every line.
choices.outcome: You get four officers and half a system, as you expected. You bid for eleven precisely so that four would look like a compromise.

choices.text: Bid exactly what you need.
choices.outcome: You get seventy per cent of exactly what you needed, because the process assumes everyone pads their bid, and punishes you for not padding.

choices.text: Don't bid. Absorb the extra work within your existing budget.
choices.outcome: Everyone above you is delighted. Your officers do the work of eleven people for three years, and two of them leave.

big: In the budget round you bid for eleven officers and get four: the reason you bid for eleven.
Budget season: every line justified, footnoted and cut by a third, as planned.
You bid big again, defend every line, and are cut back to the number you had in mind all along.
In the budget round you bid for eleven officers and a system, and get only the system, which needs eleven officers.
exact: You bid for exactly what you need and get two-thirds of it, described to you as a good outcome.
Your bid is honest and the budget is flat, and when the two meet in a spreadsheet, the spreadsheet wins.
An honest bid, funded at two-thirds again, with thanks for the realism of your projections.
Your exact bid is cut by a third, because every bid is cut by a third, and yours was exact.
absorb: You make do within your existing budget again, and a note of thanks arrives: the only increase you get.
Budget season, no bid again, and you learn one more polite way to say "we will absorb it".
No bid again. Your people absorb the extra work with you, and one of them updates a LinkedIn profile.
You absorb the extra work so quietly that next year's budget is smaller, as a vote of confidence.

variants.title: One Per Cent
variants.body: The Ministry of Finance has taken one per cent off every ministry's budget, its own included, and put it in a pot that ministries must bid for, for "new and emerging priorities". Your division needs eleven officers and a system, and since Tuesday that need has been new and emerging.

choices.text: Bid for all eleven, with a page per officer.
choices.outcome: Eleven pages, one per officer, each describing the work that officer would do. You get four back, and a note praising the pages from the people who cut them.

choices.text: Bid for exactly the gap, and say so.
choices.outcome: You bid for the gap and not a dollar more. Everyone else padded, the pot is oversubscribed, and you're funded at sixty per cent of an honest number.

choices.text: Let the one per cent go.
choices.outcome: You absorb the cut within your existing budget. Your one per cent funds someone else's new and emerging priority. Two years later that priority is merged into your division, without its officers.

variants.title: Five Minutes
variants.body: At the Permanent Secretary's budget meeting, every division's bid is on one screen, and together they add up to twice what the ministry has. Each division gets five minutes to defend its bid before the cuts are decided. Yours, for eleven officers and a system, is ninth.

choices.text: Bid big, and use every one of the five minutes.
choices.outcome: Five minutes, eleven officers, every line defended. On the spot, the Permanent Secretary trims you to four, before anyone further up can do worse, and calls it protecting you.

choices.text: Bid exactly what you need, in two minutes.
choices.outcome: You finish in two minutes. The room is so surprised that the next division overruns by six. You're funded at two-thirds, the same as everyone who padded.

choices.text: Withdraw the bid, and give back the five minutes.
choices.outcome: The meeting ends five minutes early, and the Permanent Secretary thanks you for it by name. Your people carry the extra work for two years, and one of them leaves over it.

variants.title: Tab 9
variants.body: This year's budget bid is a spreadsheet with fourteen tabs. Tab 9 is called Savings Identified, and the spreadsheet won't submit while it's blank. Your division is bidding for eleven officers and a system, and so far its savings are nil. The deadline is Friday.

choices.text: Fill tab 9 with savings you can defend, then bid big.
choices.outcome: Tab 9 finds savings in printing, travel and a hotline nobody calls. Tabs 10 to 14 spend them twice over. The bid is trimmed to four officers, as everyone expected.

choices.text: Bid what you need, and leave tab 9 honest.
choices.outcome: Tab 9 says nil, with a note explaining why. The spreadsheet won't accept a nil, so IT enters a zero for you and the note is lost. The bid is funded at two-thirds.

choices.text: Close the spreadsheet. Absorb the work within your existing budget.
choices.outcome: No bid, no tab 9. The year-end summary lists your division under "units not requiring additional resources", in a slightly larger font than the others.

title: Tuesday Night
body: It is Tuesday, the night of your weekly Meet-the-People Session, where residents bring you their problems and volunteers write appeal letters for them. Tonight there are forty-one residents, a queue to the lift lobby, and a man who has come every week for two years about a case that cannot be reopened. Parliament sits tomorrow, and your speech is half written.

choices.text: See every last one of them.
choices.outcome: You finish at 12:40am and fix the two things that could be fixed. The man will be back next Tuesday, as he will be for nine more years. You finish the speech in the car, and it sounds it.

choices.text: Take the hardest cases, and write them yourself.
choices.outcome: You write eleven letters, each argued rather than copied from a template, and three succeed that would not have. Thirty residents are seen by your volunteers, who are very good, and are not you.

choices.text: Leave at ten. Finish the speech.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten, and the speech goes well in the House. The volunteers stay until one. By Thursday a resident has posted about the evening, and the post is about what time you left.

everyone: You see every resident on Tuesday nights, and a man whose case cannot be reopened now brings you kueh, still warm from the market.
Your Meet-the-People Session runs past midnight again, and the volunteers have started bringing cushions.
The coffee shop downstairs now closes before your Meet-the-People Session does, every week.
Another Tuesday ends after midnight, with the last resident apologising for the hour and seen anyway.
A resident brings a folder of letters from three MPs before you, and you read every one.
The last resident of the night only wants to say thank you, and you stay for all forty minutes of it.
hardest: You write the hardest appeals yourself, and three a month now succeed that would not have.
An appeal you argued yourself is approved, and the resident thanks the volunteer who typed it, fairly.
You write the hard appeals yourself again, and one agency has started to recognise your paragraphs.
A letter you drafted on a Tuesday gets a reply by Friday, and the volunteers call it a record.
Your letters to agencies now open with the right section number, and the agencies have noticed.
A volunteer asks how you write the hard appeals, and you teach the paragraph, not the template.
speech: You leave the Tuesday session at ten again, and the volunteers see the rest of the queue, very well and very tired.
A resident thanks you for the new lifts, which were the Town Council's doing, and you accept on its behalf and leave at ten.
Your speech for Parliament is done by Wednesday, because the volunteers saw out the Tuesday queue without you.
You leave Meet-the-People at ten again, and the volunteers no longer look up when the lift doors close.
Your speech is the best-prepared in the House, and the Tuesday queue is a little longer for it.
The volunteers keep a list of the residents who asked for you after ten, and give it to you monthly.

variants.title: Meet-the-People, After the Rain
variants.body: Your weekly Meet-the-People Session, where residents bring you their problems: a downpour at seven, so everyone comes at nine. In the queue are a family whose flat appeal has been turned down twice, and a man who wants the void deck, the open ground floor of his block, named after his father. Parliament sits at noon tomorrow, and you have not read your papers.

choices.text: Stay until the last one is seen.
choices.outcome: Past one in the morning. The void deck will not be renamed, and you tell him so, kindly enough that he shakes your hand twice. You read your papers for the sitting in the car.

choices.text: Take the family's appeal, and write it yourself.
choices.outcome: Two pages, citing the right paragraph. The appeal succeeds on the third try, which the family credits to persistence and you credit to the paragraph. A volunteer sees the void deck man.

choices.text: Leave the volunteers to finish. Read your papers.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten and are word-perfect in the House. Your volunteers see the last resident out after midnight. The following Tuesday, the void deck man asks, pointedly, whether you are staying tonight.

variants.title: Tuesday Night, the Lift
variants.body: Thirty residents at tonight's Meet-the-People Session, all about one thing: a lift that has been under upgrading for eleven months. Nobody is angry with you. Everybody would like you to be angry on their behalf, tonight, in person. Parliament sits tomorrow, and you have papers to read.

choices.text: See every one of them, one by one.
choices.outcome: Thirty conversations about the same lift, until one in the morning. They go home feeling heard. That is not a lift, but it is not nothing.

choices.text: Write about the lift properly, tonight.
choices.outcome: Your letter names the contractor, the start date and the eleven months. A new completion date arrives within the week, and is met. Volunteers saw the residents, and the residents noticed that you did not.

choices.text: Let the volunteers take the rest.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten to prepare for the House. Twenty-nine residents are seen about the lift. The thirtieth wanted you, and mentions it at every block party for a year.

title: The Walkabout
body: It is 7:20am at the wet market in your ward, on a walkabout with a camera crew: a slow walk past every stall, meeting voters. A stallholder has strong and specific views about the price of chillies, and is delighted to share them, at volume. Fourteen stalls are still to go, and every one of them votes.

choices.text: Listen to her properly, on camera.
choices.outcome: Four minutes of her talking and you not interrupting. The clip is shared widely, and the comments are, unusually, kind. The last fourteen stalls get nine seconds each.

choices.text: Keep moving. Every stall gets a handshake.
choices.outcome: Every stall in forty minutes. The photographs are excellent, and nobody remembers a word you said.

choices.text: Take her number. Call her tonight, off camera.
choices.outcome: You call at nine. She talks for forty minutes about chillies, supply chains and her nephew. None of it is filmed, and two of her points end up in your letter to the ministry.

listen: Wet markets at 7am, with cameras, until you know the price of chillies better than the price of anything else.
On a walkabout an auntie says you looked thinner on television, and you hear out the rest of what she has to say, about her lift.
A stallholder you once heard out on camera now greets you every visit with the latest price rises.
Another walkabout, another auntie, and four minutes of footage about her lift that the news runs in full.
A fishmonger explains the price of fish to you on camera, and the clip is shared mostly by fishmongers.
You hear out a complaint about a bus route on camera, and the route is changed, though not because of the camera.
move_on: A walkabout in the rain, on schedule, and the photograph of you under someone else's umbrella does very well.
Eleven market stalls in forty minutes: everyone gets a handshake and nobody gets a sentence.
Fourteen stalls, fourteen handshakes and a volunteer one step behind you with hand sanitiser.
The walkabout keeps to time, and the photographs are better than anything anyone said.
Every stall gets a handshake before nine, and you are in the car by a quarter past, as planned.
The walkabout is so punctual that the stallholders now time their breaks by it.
call_back: You take residents' phone numbers at walkabouts and call them at night, and your call log becomes the best map of the ward.
Three phone numbers on a napkin from the wet market, and you call all three that evening, off camera.
You call a stallholder back about her rent, and she tells the next stall, and the next.
A resident you called one night tells the whole residents' committee, and the committee now knows you as the MP who calls back.
Your evening calls to residents now take longer than the walkabouts, and sort out more.
A hawker you called back about her lease tells you the next week that it was renewed, as if you did it.

variants.title: The Hawker Centre
variants.body: A lunchtime walkabout at a hawker centre in your ward, table by table, meeting voters, with photographers. The uncle at the drinks stall wants to explain, in detail, why his rent has gone up and what should be done about it. The other stalls are watching to see how long you give him.

choices.text: Sit down and hear him out.
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes, one kopi going cold, and a written follow-up on his rent. The one photographer who stayed gets the best picture of the day. The next three stalls get none of your time.

choices.text: Buy a kopi, smile, and keep moving.
choices.outcome: You pay for the kopi, smile for the photograph and move on. In the photograph, he is still talking.

choices.text: Ask for his number. Call him tonight.
choices.outcome: You call after dinner. He has prepared notes. His rent case goes to the agency under your name the next morning, and there is no photograph of any of it.

variants.title: The Estate Visit
variants.body: An estate walkabout in your ward: eight blocks before lunch, then a ribbon to cut, with cameras all the way. A resident on a mobility scooter wants to show you a ramp that does not quite reach the kerb. It is two blocks off your route, and the ribbon is on a schedule.

choices.text: Go and look at the ramp.
choices.outcome: You walk the ramp with her, slowly, cameras behind you. It is two centimetres short, and fixed within a fortnight. The ribbon is cut forty minutes late, to applause from people who wanted lunch.

choices.text: Promise someone will look, and stay on schedule.
choices.outcome: Someone does look, eventually. The ribbon is cut on time, by you, in a photograph that is very well lit.

choices.text: Get her number. Send someone this afternoon.
choices.outcome: An officer measures the ramp at four: two centimetres short. It is fixed within a fortnight. She sends you a photograph of herself using it, and nobody else ever sees it.

title: The Parliamentary Question
body: A Member has filed a Parliamentary Question about a scheme your ministry runs, and you must answer it in the House. The question is good and sharply drafted, and the honest answer is not flattering. The brief your officials wrote is accurate, and answers a slightly different question. Whatever you say goes into Hansard, the official record of Parliament, for good.

choices.text: Answer it straight, and say what you will do.
choices.outcome: You concede the point: "The scheme is not reaching the people it was built for, and we will change it by June." The follow-up question is gentler, because there is nothing left to prise open. The line goes into Hansard, word for word.

choices.text: Read the brief, which answers a nearby question.
choices.outcome: Technically responsive, substantively elsewhere. It takes skill and you have it, and the clip will stay online for longer than the scheme.

choices.text: Promise a full written answer, and write it properly.
choices.outcome: The written answer runs to four pages, with tables, and is the most complete account the ministry has ever given of the scheme. The Member reads it. So does one researcher.

straight: At Question Time you answer the question that was actually asked, and people still notice.
Seven questions this sitting, and two of your answers make the news for being short and true.
A Member files a question expecting your officials' usual reply, gets a straight answer instead, and files another.
Your straight answers are now quoted back to you in follow-up questions, so somebody read them.
You give the House the actual number, and the Member who asked has no follow-up question ready.
Your answer in the House is one paragraph shorter than the brief: you cut the paragraph that dodged.
brief: At Question Time you answer a question that was nearly the one asked.
A sharp follow-up question meets a smooth reply; Hansard records both, and the papers record the reply.
Question Time again, and the brief answers a question your officials found easier.
Your replies this sitting are smooth enough that the follow-up questions slide straight off them.
You read your officials' brief in full, accurately, and the Member asks the original question again in other words.
At Question Time you read the brief so well that nobody can quite say which question it answered.
written: Seven questions this sitting, and the full written answers follow, as promised, with tables.
Another four-page written answer, and a university researcher cites three of them in a paper, with footnotes.
Another written answer to a Parliamentary Question goes out, longer than the question and shorter than its annex.
Your written answers come with tables, and one Member starts filing questions just to get them.
Your written answer is footnoted so thoroughly that the Member who asked thanks you for the reading list.
Another question becomes another written answer, delivered on the date you promised, and that is the news.

variants.title: Question Time
variants.body: At Question Time, when Members put questions to ministers in the House, a Member asks whether your ministry will review a rule that residents complain about every week. It is already under review, but nothing is decided, and the ministry is saving the news for a press conference in March, with the Minister, a stage and a banner. What you say now goes into Hansard, the official record of Parliament, where it stays.

choices.text: Say it is under review, and what is being looked at.
choices.outcome: You say so, plainly: "Yes, it is under review, and here are the three things we are looking at." Then you name them. The Member thanks you. The press conference in March makes smaller news than it would have, banner and all.

choices.text: Say the ministry keeps all its rules under review.
choices.outcome: This is true of every rule and says nothing about this one. The Member points that out. Hansard records you both, and the press conference in March gets the headline.

choices.text: Offer the Member a full written reply once it is decided.
choices.outcome: The written reply goes out the week after the decision: three pages, complete. The Member reads all of it, and files a new question about the parts the announcement left out.

variants.title: The Supplementary
variants.body: You have answered a Parliamentary Question about your ministry, and it went well. Then the Member rises with a follow-up question, the one your officials said would not come, and your brief has nothing on it. The House is waiting, and Hansard, the official record, is recording.

choices.text: Answer it straight, without the brief.
choices.outcome: You say, "I do not have that figure, and I will not guess it in this House," then say what you do know. It is enough. Your officials send a note that reads, in full, "Well handled."

choices.text: Answer a nearby question the brief does cover.
choices.outcome: The answer is fluent, confident and about something else. The Member says, "That was not my question," and is quoted the next morning in full.

choices.text: Offer to write to the Member, and do it properly.
choices.outcome: You write two pages, with the figure you did not have to hand. The Member quotes your letter in the next debate, more kindly than you had expected.

straight.title: The Parliamentary Question, Again
straight.body: Another Parliamentary Question on one of your ministry's schemes, and again the honest answer is unflattering. Your habit in the House is to answer straight, and the Members who file questions have noticed: they file more. How you answer this one is how you'll answer them all, and Hansard keeps every word.

choices.text: Answer it straight, as you always do.
choices.outcome: You say what isn't working and what you'll change. The Member who asked has run out of follow-up questions by the second one, and your officials have stopped drafting briefs that dodge.

choices.text: Read the officials' brief this time.
choices.outcome: The brief answers a nearby question, fluently. The Member, who has heard you answer straight before, asks the question again, slowly, and Hansard records the second asking.

choices.text: Promise a full written answer instead.
choices.outcome: The written answer runs to four pages, with tables, and arrives on the date you promised. The House hears less from you this sitting, and reads more.

brief.title: The Parliamentary Question, Again
brief.body: Another Parliamentary Question on one of your ministry's schemes, and your officials' brief is ready: accurate, and about a slightly different question, like the ones before it. Your habit in the House is to read it well. How you answer this one is how you'll answer them all, and Hansard keeps every word.

choices.text: Put the brief down. Answer the question asked.
choices.outcome: You answer the question that was asked, and the House goes quiet in the way it does for something new. Your officials rewrite the next brief overnight, to fit you.

choices.text: Read the brief, as you always do.
choices.outcome: Fluent, accurate and slightly beside the point. The follow-up slides off it, as they all do, and the clip runs for a day longer than the answer deserved.

choices.text: Offer a full written answer instead.
choices.outcome: Four pages, with tables, that answer exactly what was asked. The Member is so surprised that the next question arrives with a thank-you.

written.title: The Parliamentary Question, Again
written.body: Another Parliamentary Question on one of your ministry's schemes. Your habit in the House is to promise a full written answer and deliver it, with tables, and one Member now files questions just to get them. How you answer this one is how you'll answer them all, and Hansard keeps every word.

choices.text: Answer this one straight, on your feet.
choices.outcome: You answer it in four sentences, and the House hears what your written answers have been saying all along. This time the press gallery writes it down.

choices.text: Read the brief, and save the tables.
choices.outcome: The brief answers a nearby question, and the House moves on. The Member who collects your written answers looks at an empty folder, and files another question.

choices.text: Promise the written answer, as usual.
choices.outcome: Another four pages, footnoted, on the date you promised. A researcher cites it within the month. In the House, the exchange takes eleven seconds.

title: The Ministry Townhall
body: You are hosting your ministry's townhall: four hundred officers, and an anonymous question board on the screen behind you. One question has far more upvotes than the rest. It is about workload, and it is not polite. Every officer in the room is waiting to see whether you read it out.

choices.text: Read it out and answer it.
choices.outcome: You read it in full, rude part included, and answer it for eleven minutes without notes. The room changes temperature. Nobody repeats anything else from the townhall, inside the ministry or out.

choices.text: Address the theme without reading it.
choices.outcome: You speak warmly about wellbeing and the importance of a sustainable pace. Four hundred officers understand precisely what has happened, and the question's upvotes keep climbing.

face: The workload question tops the townhall board again, you read it out again, and this time the room applauds before you answer.
Four hundred officers, one microphone, and a rude question read out in full: the only part of the townhall anyone repeats.
An officer thanks you at the lift for reading the rude townhall question out, in a whisper, in case anyone is listening.
You read the townhall's top question out in full, and the next year one officer puts a real name to a question.
The townhall question about workload is read out again, and this time a director in the front row nods.
deflect: The townhall's top question is about workload, and you address its theme, warmly.
Your townhall slides circulate, unofficially, as an example of what a townhall can be.
The townhall runs to time and the theme is addressed, while the question waits on the board like a queue number.
At the townhall you answer the theme of the top question so warmly that HR asks to use it in a module.
The theme of the top question becomes the title of next year's townhall, and that counts as an answer.

variants.title: The Curated Questions
variants.body: At your ministry's townhall this year, the questions were submitted in advance and curated, so that nothing awkward would come up. Four hundred officers are watching. An officer at the back raises a hand anyway, and the room turns to see whether you will take the question.

choices.text: Take the question.
choices.outcome: It is about promotions, and it is fair. You answer it partly, and say that it is only partly. Afterwards, the curated questions are the part nobody remembers.

choices.text: Say there will be time at the end.
choices.outcome: There is no time at the end. There was never going to be, and four hundred officers watched the hand go down.

variants.title: The Extra Floor
variants.body: You are hosting your ministry's townhall: four hundred officers and a roving microphone. An officer asks why headquarters added a floor of staff this year, while every division was told to absorb its work. It's true, the room knows it, and everyone is waiting to see what you do with it.

choices.text: Say it's true, and say why.
choices.outcome: You say it's true, and why, and that it won't happen next year. The applause is short and real. Someone in the third row writes "next year" in a notebook.

choices.text: Talk about the year's priorities.
choices.outcome: You talk about priorities for six minutes, well. The officer who asked sits down, and the microphone moves on, and the floor is still there.

title: A Year Without Incident
body: Nothing goes wrong this year. Everything you're responsible for runs, and when you go to Bintan for a week in June, nothing breaks while you're away. That means either you've set things up well, or nothing needs you. You have a year to decide which.

choices.text: Use it to fix something nobody asked you to fix.
choices.outcome: You get a process fixed that has annoyed eleven thousand people for a decade. It takes the whole year, and it's never announced.

choices.text: Use it to build your network.
choices.outcome: Coffees, lunches, and a great deal of being remembered. It isn't work. It is, unmistakably, the job.

choices.text: Use it to rest.
choices.outcome: You rest. It turns out you needed the rest more than anything needed fixing, or anyone needed lunch with you.

substance: Nothing breaks all year, which you suspect isn't a coincidence and can't prove.
You use a quiet year to fix a process that annoyed people since before you arrived, and never announce it.
You spend a quiet year fixing a form nobody asked you to fix, and three people quietly stop complaining.
A quiet year, and you clear a backlog older than anyone in the office, without telling anyone.
You fix the meeting-room booking system in a quiet year, and the queue for the big room disappears.
In a quiet year you write down a process that existed only in one retiring officer's head.
visibility: A quiet year and forty lunches, of which you remember thirty: about average.
You go to everything you're invited to, and by December you're invited to more.
A quiet year of coffees in the same three cafés, with people who will remember you as "helpful".
A quiet year of networking, after which three people you've met once describe you as "a friend".
In a quiet year you join two committees, both for the networking and one of them for the food.
A quiet year of receptions, where you learn to hold a plate, a glass and a business card at once.
low: A week on Bintan in June, where you check your email only twice. That's progress.
A quiet year, and somewhere someone writes "steady" about you and means it kindly.
A quiet year, and you take all your leave, which the leave system flags as unusual.
You rest, and everything keeps running without you. It's reassuring, and very slightly insulting.
A quiet year, and you leave at six without a single email asking where you are.
A quiet year, and you read three books, none of them about leadership.

variants.body: This year brings no crisis, no reorganisation and no question in Parliament with your name in it. Your diary has empty afternoons, something nobody around you has seen in years. Everyone has noticed, and is pretending not to. Empty afternoons get filled, and for once you can choose with what.

choices.text: Use it to fix something small and permanent.
choices.outcome: You fix the thing that has made every new joiner's first week worse for a decade. Nobody thanks you. The new joiners never find out what it used to be like.

choices.text: Use it for the lunches you keep postponing.
choices.outcome: Eleven lunches, four dinners and one kopi at a hawker centre that turns out to matter more than the dinners. People remember you now in a way they didn't.

choices.text: Use it to sleep.
choices.outcome: You sleep. Your doctor, who has been saying things for three years, says nothing at all: the nicest thing a doctor has ever said to you.

variants.body: Nothing much happens to you this year. The most discussed thing on your floor is the new coffee machine, which has nine settings; everyone uses the same one. A quiet year is a chance to do something for yourself.

choices.text: Read every file you've been forwarded and never opened.
choices.outcome: In the unopened files you find two problems you can fix, and one that someone should have fixed three years ago. You fix the two, and write a note about the third that nobody will enjoy receiving.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to the people who decide things.
choices.outcome: You become the person who knows where everything is and who to ask. It isn't a title, but it gets you into rooms.

choices.text: Take your leave, all of it.
choices.outcome: You take every day of leave you're owed. The office copes without you, which is either reassuring or not.

substance.title: Another Quiet Year
substance.body: Another year without incident: everything runs, and your diary has empty afternoons. Your quiet years have a pattern by now: you fill them by fixing things nobody asked you to fix, and say nothing about it. What you do with this one decides the quiet years after it, and nobody will ask about them again.

choices.text: Find the next thing that needs fixing.
choices.outcome: This year it's the leave form, which asked for your reason three times. It asks once now. Nobody announces it, and you've stopped expecting anyone to.

choices.text: Spend this one on lunches.
choices.outcome: Eleven lunches and a dinner, with people you've fixed things for without their knowing. Now they know, and several of them say so in rooms you're not in.

choices.text: Rest. You've earned it.
choices.outcome: You rest, and the next broken thing stays broken for the year. Someone else fixes it eventually, and is thanked for it. You sleep well anyway.

visibility.title: Another Quiet Year
visibility.body: Another year without incident, and the diary has gaps in it again. Your quiet years have a pattern by now: you fill them with coffees and lunches, and you're invited to more things than you can attend. What you do with this one decides the quiet years after it, and nobody will ask about them again.

choices.text: Turn down the lunches. Fix something instead.
choices.outcome: You decline nine invitations and fix the process that slows every new joiner's first week. Three people stop inviting you. The new joiners never find out you were busy.

choices.text: Accept everything, as usual.
choices.outcome: Forty lunches, a reception a week, and a phone full of people who call you "a friend". Some of them mean it.

choices.text: Accept nothing. Go home on time.
choices.outcome: You go home on time all year. The invitations thin out by June, and by December you can't honestly say you mind.

low.title: Another Quiet Year
low.body: Another year without incident, and nothing needs you. Your quiet years have a pattern by now: you take them as rest, your leave, all of it, and home by six. What you do with this one decides the quiet years after it, and nobody will ask about them again.

choices.text: Use this one to fix something.
choices.outcome: You find the thing that has annoyed everyone for years, and fix it by September. People are surprised it was you, and say so, which is less flattering than it sounds.

choices.text: Use this one to see people.
choices.outcome: Lunches again, after a long gap. Several people are pleased to see you, and two of them had assumed you'd left the service.

choices.text: Rest, as you always do.
choices.outcome: You take every day of leave you're owed, and the office runs without you. The leave system flags it as unusual. Nobody else does.

title: The Counter
body: You're a Management Executive at the {ministry}, eight months in. Before this you spent four years working a public service counter, and you're still finishing a part-time degree at night. Your reporting officer, {senior}, has set up a team to redesign how the public applies for a scheme. You're the most junior person on it, and the only one who has ever worked a counter.

choices.text: Tell the team exactly why the new design will fail.
choices.outcome: You describe, from memory, the eleven things a person at a counter is actually holding in their hands. The room goes quiet, and the design changes. {senior} asks where you worked before, and listens to the whole answer.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the pilot show them.
choices.outcome: The pilot fails exactly the way you knew it would, and you're the one asked to fix it. Being listened to the first time would have been less work.

title: The Last Paper
body: Your part-time degree is down to one Saturday exam, after six years of evening classes. It's also the busiest month of the year at work. {peer}, who joined the service the same year as you, finished {peer.their} degree at twenty-two, full-time, on a scholarship. Finishing yours opens jobs a diploma doesn't.

choices.text: Sit the exam and finish it.
choices.outcome: You pass, with a Second Upper. Nobody at work marks it, because nobody at work knew. But it changes which jobs you can apply for, and, more slowly, which ones you think you can.

choices.text: Defer it. Work needs you this month.
choices.outcome: The busy month is followed by another, and another. You finish the degree four years later, by which time the jobs it would have opened have gone to other people.

title: Someone From Before
body: At a meeting of several agencies, you recognise the person chairing it. Years ago, before your degree, the two of you worked side by side at a public service counter, on the same grade. Your old colleague is three grades above you now, and chairs the committees that decide who gets noticed.

choices.text: Speak to your old colleague afterwards.
choices.outcome: You're remembered at once, and without condescension, which you hadn't dared expect. Within the month you're on two committees that matter, and have been told plainly which one to care about.

choices.text: Say nothing. Your old colleague has moved on.
choices.outcome: Your old colleague hadn't moved on, and simply hadn't seen you at the far end of the table. You think about the counter for a week, and then you stop.

title: The Board Takes a Second Look
body: Someone on a promotion board has read several of your papers, and thinks your work is better than your grade suggests. Unusually, the board has been asked to look again at your file, and at HR's private estimate of the highest grade you'll ever reach, which is never shown to you.

choices.text: Make the case yourself, in writing.
choices.outcome: Four pages. You don't argue that you've been treated unfairly, which would be true and useless. You argue what you'd do with the next grade. The estimate is revised, and nobody tells you by how much.

choices.text: Let the record speak.
choices.outcome: The record does speak, in the dry language of appraisal forms, and it moves the board slightly less than four pages would have.

title: The Figure, Cited
body: A review of why your old scheme struggled has just cited a figure: 31%. That was its real usage rate, the one you put on a slide years ago instead of the range you'd been asked for. {Asker} asks, carefully, who presented it.

options.text: {senior}, who wanted the range back then,

choices.text: Say it was you.
choices.outcome: {Asker.short} nods slowly and makes a note. A month later you're asked to help redesign the scheme: the kind of request that comes before a promotion.

choices.text: Say it was a team effort.
choices.outcome: It wasn't, entirely. Your team knows that, and it does you more good with them than the other answer would have done upstairs.

title: Paragraph Four
body: When a consultancy's $1.9 million deck repeated the advice in your old minute paper, you circulated the paper to everyone at the presentation. The ministry went with the consultants' version anyway, and it has now gone wrong exactly as your paragraph four, on the risks, said it would. Someone upstairs has found paragraph four.

choices.text: Let paragraph four speak for itself.
choices.outcome: It's read aloud at a meeting you aren't at. Afterwards three people forward it to you, each believing they're the first.

choices.text: Offer to fix it.
choices.outcome: You're allowed to. It takes a year, and then a consultancy is hired to evaluate your fix.

title: The Thing Nobody Announced
body: When your division had nothing ready for the Committee of Supply, you told the Minister so early, and the Minister announced nothing. Now every ministry that did announce something is explaining delays. Your Minister is the only one who isn't, and has noticed why.

choices.text: Bring the Minister the pilot, now that it's ready.
choices.outcome: It's announced at the next Committee of Supply, on time and as described. The Minister mentions your division by name, something Ministers almost never do.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let the Minister draw the conclusion.
choices.outcome: The Minister draws it. When the Permanent Secretary next asks which divisions the Minister rates, yours is named first, in front of the person who writes your ranking.

title: The Raw Feedback
body: A think tank has analysed the raw feedback you published alongside your national conversation report, back when nobody had done that. Its paper is quoted approvingly in Parliament by both sides. It reaches you from the Permanent Secretary's office, forwarded with no comment at all, which from that office is a great deal of comment.

choices.text: Reply with one line.
choices.outcome: "Thank you. It was their feedback." The reply comes back within a minute, which nobody on your floor has ever seen the Permanent Secretary do.

choices.text: Write the follow-up nobody asked for.
choices.outcome: The next national conversation uses your follow-up as its template, and this time nobody announces the pillars until the feedback is in.

title: The Decision Paper
body: When you were secretariat to a deadlocked Inter-Ministry Committee, you wrote a paper that forced it to decide. That committee has now been dissolved, and its replacement has adopted your paper as its terms of reference. The footer still says "Prepared by {player.full}, Secretariat", and the paper is about to go to every ministry.

choices.text: Leave your name on it.
choices.outcome: The footer travels further than you ever have. A Deputy Secretary you've never met asks for you by name.

choices.text: Take it off before it circulates.
choices.outcome: It circulates without a name, and in this building that's how everyone finds out who wrote it.

title: The Third Point
body: Some time ago, a viral post about your ministry's scheme got two points wrong and one right, and you publicly admitted the one it got right. Now the scheme has been quietly amended to fix exactly that. {journalist}, {journalist.aTitle} at the paper, has noticed that you were the only office holder who admitted it, and asks about it on the record.

choices.text: Take the question on the record.
choices.outcome: The piece runs on a Sunday, headlined "{player.formal} candid on scheme flaw". Candid is a word your press secretary asks you never to be again.

choices.text: Credit the post's author.
choices.outcome: The post's author is astonished, then gracious, then a reliable critic of yours for the rest of your career. You decide to take that as a compliment.

title: Hansard
body: Years ago you stood up in the House and said plainly what you thought, when a safer version was ready in front of you. Your words went into Hansard, word for word. This week a newer Member quotes them in a speech, beginning "As {player.full} said in this House". Someone on the front bench, where the ministers sit, looks up the original, and so does the press gallery.

choices.text: Send the newer Member a note.
choices.outcome: The note is framed. You hear about this from four people, none of whom is the Member who framed it.

choices.text: Say nothing.
choices.outcome: The quote goes round without you. It turns out to be the most-shared thing you've ever said, and it's years old.

title: Terms of Reference
body: Some years ago you asked the other ministers whether ministers should be paid on targets they can move themselves. Now a committee has been appointed to review political salaries, and your question appears, unattributed, as item three of its terms of reference. The committee is inviting submissions.

choices.text: Make a submission under your own name.
choices.outcome: The committee thanks you for your submission. Its report adjusts the formula by one percentage point, which it describes as significant. Your name is in the annex, where colleagues will find it.

choices.text: Let item three do the work.
choices.outcome: Item three does very little work on its own. But you were seen not to make a fuss, and among colleagues that counts for something.

title: The Annual Report
body: You were seconded to a statutory board in trouble, to fix it, without knowing whether the posting was a proving ground or a siding. Its new annual report is out: for the first time in four years the accounts needed no corrections, and the auditors' letter is one page long. Your secondment is ending, and you can ask to come back or to stay.

choices.text: Ask to come back.
choices.outcome: You come back to a better office than the one you left. So it was a proving ground after all. Nobody says so; everyone simply acts as if it had always been obvious.

choices.text: Ask to stay and finish it.
choices.outcome: You stay. The board becomes a case study on the leadership programme, taught by someone who was never there.

title: Polling Day, Again
body: Parliament is dissolved on a Tuesday, so there is a general election within weeks and your seat is up again. Lose it, and your political career is over. Nobody is surprised: the party's tents went up under the blocks a fortnight ago. This time the chairman of your party branch, which runs the party's volunteers in your ward, has started using the word "swing" in sentences about you.

choices.text: Campaign on the record.
choices.outcome: You stand on a campaign lorry and read out everything the ward got since the last election, as if it were all your doing. Some of it was.

choices.text: Walk every block, every night, for nine days.
choices.outcome: Nine nights, four hundred lift lobbies, and one pair of shoes you will never wear again.

lines: Another general election. On the campaign lorry you read out everything the ward got in five years: new lifts, a covered walkway, an upgraded hawker centre. You read it all out as if it were your doing, and the lorry driver, who has heard every version of it, nods in the right places.
After the vote, an open lorry carries you round the ward to thank voters, by the same route as last time, down to the same coffee shop.
Nine days of campaigning, one rally, and on election night a sample count, an early tally from a few ballot boxes, that tells everyone the result before the real one does.
Your ward's result is among the first announced, and your volunteers treat this as a personal achievement.
Election posters go up at the first permitted minute and come down by the date on the permit.
On Cooling-off Day, the day before the vote, nobody may campaign, so you spend it reading the comments online, and wish you could reply.
Nomination Day, when the candidates file their papers, then nine days of walkabouts, and a result your campaign manager predicted, in writing, to within a point.
By the end of the campaign you can rank every coffee shop in the ward by its kopi, privately.

variants.body: The general election is called in the middle of the monsoon, and your seat is contested again. Lose it, and your political career ends with it. Your volunteers have done the sums on last time's result and stopped joking about them, which is how you know the ward is close.

choices.outcome: You set out what the ward got since the last election at every rally, under a tarpaulin that drips on the front row. The front row stays anyway.
You walk the blocks in the rain for nine nights and learn which lift lobbies flood. Residents remember the umbrella longer than anything you said under it.

variants.body: Parliament is dissolved, and this time the opposition has sent your ward its best candidate: younger than you, fluent, and already photographed with every hawker in the market. Your seat is up, and losing it would end your political career. Your branch chairman has pinned the opponent's leaflet above the photocopier.

choices.outcome: You hold a press conference with a table of numbers: new lifts, new ramps, a new bus service. Your opponent holds one with a hawker, and gets the better photograph.
You visit every stall in the market twice and buy something at each. By Polling Day you have eaten more chicken rice than in the five years before it put together.

variants.body: The electoral boundaries are redrawn before the general election, and your ward gains four blocks you have never visited. Your seat is up again; lose it, and your political career is over. The new blocks' residents' committee has already written to ask who you are.

choices.outcome: You campaign on what the old blocks got since the last election. The new blocks listen politely, and then ask what they will get.
You walk the four new blocks first, every floor, and by the second night the residents' committee chairman is walking with you, mainly to tell you which doors not to knock on after nine.

variants.body: The general election falls in the month the bus service your ward has relied on for decades is withdrawn. Your seat is up, and if you lose it your political career is over. The decision was not yours, but the only face at the bus stop is yours, on an election poster.

choices.outcome: You campaign on everything else the ward got since the last election, which is a great deal. Every question at every rally is about the bus.
You ride the replacement service every morning for nine days and talk to everyone on it. It is slower than the old one, and by the end, so are you.

variants.body: A general election is called, your seat is up again, and losing it would end your political career. This time there is also a video: you, at a community event, mid-sentence, looking bored. It is eleven seconds long, and everyone in the ward seems to have seen it.

choices.outcome: You put the whole speech online, all forty minutes of it, so voters can see the eleven seconds in context. Eleven people watch it to the end.
You walk every block for nine days and let residents see you wide awake. Several tell you that you look much better in person, which you decide to count as support.

variants.body: Parliament is dissolved, and your seat is contested again; if it goes, so does your political career. Your longest-serving volunteer, who has worked on every campaign since before you arrived, has made a wall chart of every block and its mood. Too many of the blocks are coloured yellow.

choices.outcome: You give the same speech at every rally, listing what the ward got since the last election. By the last night your volunteer can mouth it along with you, and does.
You and your volunteer walk the yellow blocks first, every night for nine days. By the end the chart has more green on it, mostly in your volunteer's handwriting.

title: The National Bonus
body: Growth is strong, and your ministry must settle its plan for the next three Budgets. The plan moves the national targets your National Bonus is paid on, and you can push one of them, not all.

choices.text: Push headline GDP.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Growth comes in a little under forecast, which in a strong year is noticed, and your National Bonus drops to two months. The commentary uses the word "moderate" four times.

choices.outcome: Growth comes in above forecast, and your National Bonus is five months. The lowest incomes rise too, slightly, the way a small boat rises when a larger one goes past.

choices.text: Push the incomes of the lowest-paid.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The lowest-incomes figure misses its target by a tenth of a point, and the formula pays no National Bonus at all. Your officials' chart of it is still a good chart.

choices.outcome: The lowest incomes grow faster than the median, which has not happened in six years, and your bonus is four months. The chart goes into the Budget speech, in colour.

choices.text: Bank the targets. Change nothing that is working.
choices.outcome: Every target is met to the decimal place, which pays the standard three months. Nothing is announced, because nothing has changed, and other ministries copy the plan.

headline.title: The National Bonus, Again
headline.body: Growth is strong, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you funded the policy that lifts GDP, and your officials have redrafted it with the dates changed in pen. Whatever you sign now becomes the ministry's standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, in good years and bad, without coming back to you.

choices.text: Sign it as it is.
choices.outcome: Signed in pen, beside the old dates. Growth comes in above forecast again, your bonus is five months, and the plan will now renew itself. Nobody asks what else it could have been.

choices.text: Cross it out. Put the lowest incomes first.
choices.outcome: Your officials redraft the whole plan in a fortnight, and Finance asks in writing why a working plan has changed. The lowest incomes outgrow the median by spring, and this is now the standing plan.

choices.text: Cross it out. Bank the targets instead.
choices.outcome: The new plan is the old one with its ambitions removed, and Finance minutes it as a "recalibration". The targets are met exactly, for the standard three months, and from now on the plan renews itself.

lowest.title: The National Bonus, Again
lowest.body: Growth is strong, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you funded the policy that lifts the lowest incomes, and a chart of their rise now hangs in the ministry lobby, framed. Your officials' draft keeps it climbing. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, without being put to you again.

choices.text: Take the chart down. Push headline GDP this time.
choices.outcome: The chart comes down on a Saturday, so nobody sees it go. Growth comes in above forecast, and growth-first is now the standing plan. The officials who drew the chart ask, in a long email, what it was for.

choices.text: Sign it. Keep the chart climbing.
choices.outcome: Signed without a meeting. The lowest incomes outgrow the median for another cycle, your bonus is four months, and the plan will now roll on by itself. The lobby chart is replaced by a larger one.

choices.text: Bank the targets. Let the chart level off.
choices.outcome: The new plan meets its targets and moves nothing, and it is now the plan for good. The chart levels off and comes down, the lobby gets a potted plant, and Finance writes to say it liked the chart.

steady.title: The National Bonus, Again
steady.body: Growth is strong, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you asked the other ministers whether ministers should be paid on targets they can move, and funded neither policy. Your ministry's plan has moved none of the targets since, and your officials have drafted it again. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget without coming back to you.

choices.text: Change it. Push headline GDP while the going is good.
choices.outcome: Growth comes in above forecast, your bonus is five months, and growth-first is now the standing plan. Your question is still in Cabinet's minutes. Nobody brings it up.

choices.text: Change it. Put the lowest incomes first.
choices.outcome: The lowest incomes outgrow the median by the next survey, and that is the standing plan from now on. Your bonus rises with them. You do not ask about it a second time.

choices.text: Let it renew.
choices.outcome: It renews, and will keep renewing. The targets are met to the decimal, for the standard three months, and the plan is cited in a training course as an example of what a plan should be. It is cited nowhere else.

headline: Growth is strong, and your ministry rolls its growth-first plan into three more Budgets without asking you, as agreed.
Your officials renew the growth-first plan on their own, exactly as you told them to.
Two more plants are brought forward under your growth-first plan, announced in a press release copied from the last one.
In a strong year your standing plan pushes headline growth again, and the quarterly slide keeps its arrow pointing up.
The growth-first plan renews itself for three more Budgets, and the only edit anyone makes is to the year.
lowest: Your plan for the lowest incomes rolls into three more Budgets, and its chart gets new numbers.
Wage support for the lowest-paid is renewed without a meeting, the surest sign that it is policy now.
Finance's yearly letter asking whether the support for the lowest-paid is temporary arrives on schedule, and gets a template reply.
Your standing plan puts the lowest incomes first again, and your economists print the chart on A3, out of habit.
Another ministry adopts your plan for the lowest incomes, and sends a thank-you note with its own logo on it.
steady: The safe plan rolls into three more Budgets, and nobody in the ministry remembers a time before it.
The plan that changes nothing is renewed, unchanged, as intended.
Growth is strong and your standing plan stays steady: the targets are tracked to the decimal and nothing is announced.
Your officials renew the steady plan, and a training course adds it to its slide titled "Good Practice".
The steady plan renews itself for three more Budgets, and its only new feature is a page number.

title: The National Bonus, in a Downturn
body: Exports are down for a third quarter and "retrenchment" is back in the papers. Your ministry must settle its plan for the next three Budgets now, and in a downturn the country will miss at least one of the targets your National Bonus is paid on. You choose what to protect.

choices.text: Protect jobs first.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Unemployment rises anyway, by less than it would have. The indicator does not record the difference, and the formula pays no National Bonus.

choices.outcome: Unemployment holds, growth does not, and your bonus is two months. A great many people keep jobs they will never know were on a list.

choices.text: Push growth through it.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The push does not take. Growth stays flat, the lowest incomes fall, and there is no National Bonus. Nobody calls it a gamble, because it was a plan.

choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region and your bonus is four months. The speech about resilience writes itself. The jobs do come back, in time, in other industries, for other people.

choices.text: Cushion the lowest incomes.
