nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The cushion holds the lowest incomes steady. The indicator only counts growing, not holding steady, so the formula pays no National Bonus.

choices.outcome: The lowest incomes hold steady through the downturn, and your bonus is one month. Rent is paid on time in a great many flats. Nobody reports on rent paid on time.

steady.title: The National Bonus, Again, in a Downturn
steady.body: The economy has turned down, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you asked the other ministers whether ministers should be paid on targets they can move, and funded neither policy. So your officials' draft chases no target: it only holds on to jobs, under a cover that says "For signature", not "For decision". Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan.

choices.text: Sign it. Jobs first.
choices.outcome: Unemployment holds through the downturn, your bonus is two months, and jobs-first is now the plan for good. The cover is changed to "For information".

choices.text: Write "For decision" on it. Push growth through.
choices.outcome: Projects are brought forward, growth recovers ahead of the region, and growth-first is the standing plan from now on. Your officials, who had expected a signature, spend March rebuilding the plan around cranes.

choices.text: Write "For decision" on it. Cushion the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The cash for the lowest incomes goes out in spring, rent is paid on time in a great many flats, and this is now the standing plan. Finance asks, twice, why the plan changed.

headline.title: The National Bonus, Again, in a Downturn
headline.body: Exports have turned down, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you funded the GDP policy, and your ministry now has a growth unit, with a logo. Its draft pushes growth through the downturn. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, without coming back to you. The unit would like to continue existing.

choices.text: Overrule the unit. Protect jobs first.
choices.outcome: Unemployment holds and growth does not, and jobs-first is now the standing plan. The growth unit is renamed the Resilience Unit, in a memo that takes eleven drafts, and nobody in it is retrenched.

choices.text: Sign it. The unit knows what it is doing.
choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region again, your bonus is four months, and the plan will now renew itself. The unit's logo goes on the Budget slide, and the unit goes on existing.

choices.text: Turn the unit to the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The growth unit spends the downturn delivering cash to the lowest incomes, efficiently and with visible reluctance. Rent is paid on time in a great many flats, and this is the standing plan now.

lowest.title: The National Bonus, Again, in a Downturn
lowest.body: The downturn is official, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you funded the policy for the lowest incomes, and the payment system built for it is still running, idle, at some expense. Your officials' draft switches it back on. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, without coming back to you.

choices.text: Repurpose it for wage support, to keep people in work.
choices.outcome: The system is repurposed for wage support, which takes four months and a new acronym. Unemployment holds, jobs-first is now the standing plan, and the vendor bills for the acronym.

choices.text: Switch it off. Push growth through.
choices.outcome: Projects are brought forward, growth recovers ahead of the region, and growth-first is the plan from now on. The idle payment system is switched off, and its vendor invoices, politely, for that too.

choices.text: Sign it. Switch it back on.
choices.outcome: The cash goes out within a week, because the system remembered how. The lowest incomes hold steady, your bonus is one month, and nobody writes about a system that worked twice.

steady: A downturn, and your standing jobs-first plan comes out of a folder labelled "Downturn" that nobody has to look for.
Wage support for jobs is renewed for three more Budgets, and firms fill in the same forms, in triplicate, again.
Retrenchment is back in the papers, and your ministry's jobs scheme is back in the Budget, unchanged.
The downturn plan keeps jobs first, announced in last cycle's press release with the year changed.
headline: In a downturn your standing plan pushes growth through it again, and the cranes go up in the west on schedule.
Your growth-first plan is rolled over into the downturn, with a new cover that says "Resilience".
Projects are brought forward again, from a list that has not changed since the last downturn.
Exports fall and your ministry pushes growth anyway, as the standing plan says, with a speech about resilience.
lowest: The cash for the lowest incomes goes out again within a week of the Budget, as your standing plan says.
Your standing plan cushions the lowest incomes through another downturn, and again nobody reports on rent paid on time.
The plan for the lowest incomes is renewed through the downturn, and Finance asks once, out of habit, whether it is temporary.
The downturn cash goes out in March under your standing plan, and is spent on rent, school shoes and hawker food.

title: The National Bonus, Before an Election
body: A general election is due within the year, and your ministry must settle its plan for the next three Budgets before Nomination Day, when the candidates file their papers. The plan moves your National Bonus. The chairman of your party branch, which runs the party's volunteers in your ward, has sent, unasked, a list of what the ward would like announced.

choices.text: Spread the gains widely before polling day.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The measures land after the indicators are measured, so your bonus is one month. Residents like the measures anyway; the indicators were not voting.

choices.outcome: The measures land in time and are felt in every block, and your bonus is three months. Your branch chairman reads them out at the community club dinner, from a printout, with feeling.

choices.text: Hold the line on the targets.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The targets are nearly met, for a bonus of two months, and the campaign is a little quieter than your branch would like.

choices.outcome: The targets are met and your bonus is four months. Your branch chairman asks, politely, whether anything at all could be announced, and is sent the targets.

choices.text: Push the incomes of the lowest-paid.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The lowest-incomes figure misses its target by a tenth of a point, and the formula pays no National Bonus. In an election year, a tenth of a point gets a press conference.

choices.outcome: The lowest incomes outgrow the median, and your bonus is three months. The chart is on a campaign flyer by Friday, cropped so the axis starts somewhere encouraging.

headline.title: The National Bonus, Again, Before an Election
headline.body: A general election is due, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you put your ministry's money behind GDP, and your party branch, the volunteers who run your campaign, has reprinted the flyer that boasted about the growth. Your officials' draft matches the flyer, with measures every block will feel before polling day. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan.

choices.text: Run it as written.
choices.outcome: The measures land before polling day, in every block, with the flyer, and this is now the standing plan. At a walkabout a resident says it is the same flyer as last time, and she is right.

choices.text: Pull the flyer. Hold the line on the targets.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, the flyers are pulped, and the safe plan is the standing plan from now on. Your branch chairman asks, twice, whether the change could have waited until after polling day.

choices.text: Pull the flyer. Put the lowest incomes first.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day, a new flyer is printed with a new chart, and that is the plan from now on. The old flyers are used, unofficially, to wrap cakes at the community club.

steady.title: The National Bonus, Again, Before an Election
steady.body: An election is due, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you asked the other ministers whether ministers should be paid on targets they can move. Your officials' plan moves no target, and its annex on timing is blank. Your party branch, the volunteers who run your campaign, asks by voice note what is in it for the ward. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan.

choices.text: Fill the annex. Bring the visible measures forward.
choices.outcome: The measures land before polling day, and visible measures first is the standing plan now. Your officials redo the annex over a weekend, and Finance asks why a plan that met its targets needs a timing annex at all.

choices.text: Sign it, blank annex and all.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, your bonus is four months, and the plan will now renew itself. The branch sends a second voice note, mostly a sigh, and the campaign leads on lift upgrading instead.

choices.text: Fill the annex. The lowest incomes, before polling day.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day, and that is the standing plan now. The branch sends a thumbs-up, the first in years, and asks for a chart of it in three more languages.

lowest.title: The National Bonus, Again, Before an Election
lowest.body: Polling day is within the year, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you put your ministry's money behind the lowest incomes, and they rose. Your party branch, the volunteers who run your campaign, wants a chart of the rise on its flyer. Your officials' draft carries the same policy on, under a covering note that calls it "settled policy". Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan.

choices.text: Unsettle it. Spread the gains wider before polling day.
choices.outcome: The measures reach every block in time, and visible measures first is the standing plan from now on. Your officials refile the "settled policy" note under a heading that no longer applies.

choices.text: Unsettle it. Hold the line on the targets.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, the flyer has nothing new on it, and the safe plan is the standing plan from now on. Your branch chairman reads the covering note aloud at a meeting, slowly, as evidence.

choices.text: Leave it settled.
choices.outcome: The lowest incomes outgrow the median again, your bonus is three months, and the plan now renews itself. The chart goes on the flyer. The residents on the chart did not need the flyer to tell them.

headline: An election is due, and your standing plan brings the visible measures forward again, with last time's flyer redated.
Polling day approaches, and your ministry's measures are timed to land in every block, as the standing plan says.
Your branch gets its flyer, its measures and its press conference, in the usual order.
An election year, and the plan is rolled forward to land just before the campaign starts.
steady: An election is due, and your standing plan holds the line on the targets again; your branch chairman has stopped asking.
The safe plan rolls into an election year, and your branch learns of it from the newspapers, as usual.
Before polling day your ministry announces nothing new, on schedule.
The targets are kept through another election year, and the campaign leads on lift upgrading instead.
lowest: An election is due, and the lowest-incomes chart goes on the flyer, cropped so the axis starts somewhere encouraging.
Support for the lowest incomes is timed to land before polling day, as your standing plan says.
Your branch prints the lowest-incomes chart again, and residents on it say they did not need the flyer.
The plan for the lowest incomes renews itself in an election year, and a volunteer translates the chart's caption again.

title: The Recruiter
body: A recruiter has found you on LinkedIn, which you'd forgotten you were on. A bank wants someone who understands how ministries think, and the salary is a number you read twice. Taking it means resigning from the service, and from whatever it had planned for you.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your pass stops working on a Friday. On Monday you have a new one, and a view.

choices.text: Mention the offer, lightly, to HR.
choices.outcome: The service doesn't match a bank's offer: your pay stays what your grade pays. HR quietly raises its private estimate of how far you'll go. Your bosses hear you were shopping around, and it shows in this year's appraisal.

choices.text: Decline. You're not finished here.
choices.outcome: You delete the message. Then you undelete it, read the number again, and delete it.

title: The Consultancy
body: A consultancy, the kind that charges a ministry $1.9 million for a deck, wants to hire someone who knows what ministries actually want. Apparently that's you. Accepting means resigning from the service near the top of it. The offer letter is on very good paper.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your first engagement is with your old ministry. The slides are beautiful, and they say what your memos used to say.

choices.text: Decline, and tell them why.
choices.outcome: They take it well, and quote you in a thought-leadership piece about public-sector talent.

choices.text: Decline, and keep the letter in a drawer.
choices.outcome: The drawer is the top one. You open it more often than you'd admit.

title: The Board Seat
body: A conglomerate wants {post.ask} on its board: four meetings a year, and a fee its annual report puts in a footnote. The chairman knows you hold office, and asks only whether you might be free "after". Saying yes means leaving politics at the next election.

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} At the election a new candidate wins your old seat. The board seat, as promised, has been kept warm.

choices.text: Decline.
choices.outcome: You decline in writing. You later learn that your letter is framed in the chairman's office, as a curiosity.

options.ask: someone who has worked close to Cabinet
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister you will not stand again.
options.exit: The Prime Minister asks you to see out the term, and you do.

options.ask: someone who has run part of a ministry
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister you will not stand again.
options.exit: Your portfolio goes to a colleague who has waited for it, politely.

options.ask: someone who has sat in Cabinet
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister this Cabinet is your last.
options.exit: The reshuffle announcement thanks you in its second paragraph.

variants.body: At a charity dinner, a company chairman you have met twice steers you to the window. His board needs {post.ask}, once you are out of office. Saying yes means leaving politics at the next election. He names the fee quietly, then again, in case you were being polite.

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} A new candidate holds your seat at the election. Flowers arrive at your first board meeting, the first of four that year.

choices.text: Thank him, and decline.
choices.outcome: You decline at the window, smiling. He says the offer will keep, and every Chinese New Year a card arrives to show that it is keeping.

variants.body: A search firm writes, on paper thick enough to stand up by itself, about a client's board seat for {post.ask}, from "a date convenient to you": after you leave politics. Saying yes means not standing again. The fee is in the second paragraph. The second paragraph is short.

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} Your seat passes to a new candidate. The search firm's next letter begins "Dear Director", and is much thinner.

choices.text: Decline, on your own letterhead.
choices.outcome: The search firm replies within the hour to thank you, and files you under "later". The list of people filed under "later" is long, and well looked after.

choices.outcome: The search firm replies within the hour to thank you, and files you under "later". The list of people filed under "later" is long, and well looked after.

title: The Citizens' Panel
body: Years ago a retired schoolteacher wrote an angry, accurate letter to the Forum page about your scheme, and you looked up his address in the ministry's records. Now twelve members of the public, picked at random, are reviewing the scheme over three Saturdays. He's one of them, and he has brought the cutting.

choices.text: Tell him, privately, that you once looked up his address.
choices.outcome: He considers this for a long time, then says that in thirty years of teaching he looked up many pupils' addresses, usually because he was worried about them, and he hopes you were at least that worried. The panel's report is fair. He wrote most of it.

choices.text: Thank him for his letter, in front of the panel.
choices.outcome: He accepts the thanks with the face of a teacher accepting homework that has clearly been copied. The panel's report is fair, and has a section on responsiveness.

choices.text: Leave the sessions to {junior}.
choices.outcome: {junior} reports back that the panel was constructive, and that one member asked, twice, whether you'd be coming.

title: The Promotion Board
body: Years ago, when your division was moved to another ministry, you fought for your nine officers' postings before your own. The sharpest of them, then a young assistant director, is a Director now, and sits on the four-person board deciding your promotion. No interest has been declared, because the form has no box for gratitude.

choices.text: Ask HR whether this needs declaring.
choices.outcome: HR checks its guidance, which covers family, money and former employers but not gratitude, and to be safe replaces your old officer with someone who has never heard of you. The board is very fair. You find this less comforting than you expected.

choices.text: Say nothing. It isn't a conflict; it's a memory.
choices.outcome: Your old officer says very little in the board itself, having said it all at lunch beforehand, to the chair, in one sentence about a reorganisation.

title: A Small Favour
body: Years ago your friend at HDB told you about a flat launch three weeks before it was public, and you got your flat. Now your friend has been in touch: a nephew has applied for a job in the civil service. The nephew is very hardworking, your friend says, and wants no special treatment, only for someone to look at the application.

choices.text: Make sure someone looks at it.
choices.outcome: Someone looks at it. The nephew is interviewed, turns out to be very hardworking, and gets the job on merit, probably. The flat and the nephew are now one story, and it's yours.

choices.text: Forward it to HR, declaring the connection.
choices.outcome: HR thanks you for declaring it, and files the declaration next to the application. The nephew isn't shortlisted. Your friend says it's understood, in the tone of someone updating a ledger.

choices.text: Say you can't, and why.
choices.outcome: You mention the flat. There's a pause on the line, then a laugh: that was public information, three weeks early. You agree that it was. Neither of you mentions the nephew again.

title: The Block Party
body: Years ago, before politics, you spent a year of Tuesday nights writing appeal letters at a Meet-the-People Session. One letter, for a woman everyone said was hopeless, won. Now, at a block party in your ward, that woman is introducing you to forty of her neighbours. She has told them the story, in detail, more than once.

choices.text: Let her tell it again.
choices.outcome: She tells it with improvements. By the end of the evening the appeal has overturned a decision, saved a business and possibly a marriage. Forty people will vote for the version with the marriage.

choices.text: Tell them the appeal worked because her case was good.
choices.outcome: This is true. She tells them you are being modest, and now the modesty is part of the story too. It goes round the block faster than you can walk it.

title: The Budget Committee
body: In the reorganisation years ago, you took the good box, the one director-level post, that {peer} was about to get. {peer} has had a perfectly good career anyway, and now chairs the committee that decides your division's budget. {peer} is scrupulously fair to you, and somehow that's worse.

choices.text: Apologise, properly, over coffee.
choices.outcome: {peer} lets you finish, then says {peer.they} stopped thinking about it years ago, which you both know is the kind of thing people say. Your budget is approved in full. You'll never know whether the coffee helped.

choices.text: Make your bid on its merits and nothing else.
choices.outcome: It's a good bid, and it gets exactly what a good bid gets from someone being scrupulously fair: four officers and half a system.

choices.text: Find out who else sits on the committee.
choices.outcome: Two of the other four remember the reorganisation too, and one of them owes you. You spend a week arranging to be owed slightly more, and the bid passes.

title: Farewell Drinks
body: Your friend in HR, the one who explained your CEP to you over lunch years ago, is leaving the service. At the farewell drinks, on a second glass, your friend tells you how yours gets reviewed: every year, by people who mostly read your last two postings, and who like officers who have run something, not just written about it. So far, yours have all been papers.

choices.text: Ask to run something at your next posting.
choices.outcome: You ask the next morning. HR says it will note your interest, and does: your next posting comes with nine officers, a hotline and a backlog, and it gets read twice.

choices.text: Say thanks, and let your friend enjoy the drinks.
choices.outcome: You talk about your friend's new job instead: a bank, at a salary that had to be read twice.

title: The Interview Panel
body: You've known for years that {peer} was the one who leaked a confidential policy to a Telegram channel: you worked it out quietly, and told nobody. {peer} has done well since, and is now on the interview panel for a post you want. {peer} doesn't know that you know. You're almost sure of this.

choices.text: Say nothing. Compete on the record.
choices.outcome: {peer} asks you two fair questions and one hard one, and you answer all three. Whether {peer} knows that you know is still, as far as you can tell, something only you lie awake over.

choices.text: Let {peer} understand, very quietly, that you know.
choices.outcome: You mention, in passing, a Telegram channel. {peer} doesn't react at all, and that's how you know it landed. You get the post. You also have a colleague who now depends on your silence, and won't forgive you for saying so.

title: Two Names
body: The "Enhanced" scheme your division announced at Committee of Supply was an old scheme renamed, so the Minister had something new to say. {journalist} has now noticed that it has the same budget, the same rules and the same hotline as the scheme it replaced, and would like to know which name people should use when they call.

choices.text: Say both names are correct.
choices.outcome: {journalist.formal} prints that both names are correct. It reads exactly as well as it sounds.

choices.text: Say it's the same scheme, renamed, and explain what changed.
choices.outcome: What changed was the word "Enhanced", and you say so. The headline is "Only the name has changed, says {player.formal}", and the piece is, against all expectation, quite kind.

title: The Raw Data
body: When you wrote up the national conversation, you spread its feedback across three pillars, though most of it was about the cost of living. Now a think tank has asked, politely, for the raw feedback. The spreadsheet is still in a file, and it still doesn't fit three pillars.

choices.text: Release it.
choices.outcome: The think tank's paper observes, politely, that the feedback and the report describe two different countries. Days later the Permanent Secretary asks why you released it. You say it was asked for. That, you're told, isn't usually the reason.

choices.text: Send the report again, with a covering note.
choices.outcome: Your covering note is very good. The think tank thanks you for the report, which it already had, and files a formal request for the data instead.

title: Officer A
body: When you stepped off a tender panel because the bidder was an old colleague, you wrote a one-page memo saying why. That memo is now slide 14 of the procurement course every new officer takes. It doesn't name you; it calls you Officer A. At lunch, {junior} tells another officer about Officer A, approvingly, in front of you.

choices.text: Tell them it was you.
choices.outcome: They're delighted, and then slightly disappointed, the way people are when a parable turns out to be someone they report to.

choices.text: Say nothing, and finish your lunch.
choices.outcome: Officer A stays a better person than you, because Officer A never has to do anything else. You find you don't mind.

title: Lanterns
body: The grassroots adviser who told you at a lift lobby that you handle yourself well with people has been in touch, as promised. Are you free on Saturday? It is the community club's Mid-Autumn celebration, with lanterns, a lion dance and the local Member of Parliament, and the MP would like to meet you. This, the adviser says, is nothing formal.

choices.text: Go, and stay to stack the chairs.
choices.outcome: You carry lanterns, are photographed with a lion, and stack chairs until ten. The MP talks to you for five minutes and notices the chairs, and the party now has a note on you.

choices.text: Send your apologies. You have a deadline.
choices.outcome: The deadline is met. The adviser says there will be other Saturdays, in the tone of someone writing down which ones.

title: The First Cabinet
body: The colleague you backed for the succession, instead of standing yourself, is now Prime Minister. At the first Cabinet meeting the new Prime Minister thanks everyone for their support, in general terms, and then looks at you for slightly longer than at anyone else. You are owed something, and everyone at the table can see it.

choices.text: Ask for nothing.
choices.outcome: You are given something anyway: the chair of a ministerial committee that meets on Saturday mornings. The appointment is a sign of enormous trust, and you will never see a Saturday again.

choices.text: Ask, at the table, for the portfolio you were promised.
choices.outcome: The Prime Minister gives it to you before the next item on the agenda, and the whole table watches a debt being paid in full. It's a good portfolio. Everyone will remember how you got it.

title: The Other Life
body: You declined the party's invitation to tea, years ago, when it wanted to sound you out about politics. Someone invited the same year went, and is now a Minister. On the evening news, that Minister announces a scheme your people designed, and thanks the public service, correctly, in general terms.

choices.text: Send the Minister a note of congratulations.
choices.outcome: The Minister replies by hand, remembering the year you were both invited, and admitting to having wondered ever since which of you chose right. The reply doesn't say which way the Minister has decided.

choices.text: Turn off the television and go back to the file.
choices.outcome: The file is better than the announcement. It usually is. That was, you remind yourself, more or less why you said no.

title: The Younger Officer
body: Years ago the party invited you to tea too. At the background check that followed, you told them everything, including what wasn't in their folder on you, and you never heard from the party again. Now a younger officer, just invited to tea, asks you over kopi whether to go, and knows none of this.

choices.text: Say go, and keep the folder thin.
choices.outcome: The younger officer goes. Two years later there is a new candidate in the newspapers, crediting an older colleague with the best advice of a career, and not saying what it was. That's the advice working.

choices.text: Tell the younger officer about your folder.
choices.outcome: You tell all of it. The younger officer listens the way you once listened at tea, thanks you, and you realise you've just been vetted by someone half your age.

title: A Model Ward
body: Your ward's six-point swing towards you at the election, the best result in the region, has reached an internal party paper. It calls your ward a model and credits "{player.full} and {player.their} walkabouts". The party's organising secretary wants you to mentor three new candidates. You suspect the swing was really three things: the volunteers, the Tuesday-night Meet-the-People Sessions where residents queue with their problems, and a weak opponent.

choices.text: Teach them the walkabout, as the paper says.
choices.outcome: You teach them to listen to a stallholder on camera without looking like someone listening on camera. Two of them get it. The paper is reprinted with their photographs.

choices.text: Teach them Meet-the-People on Tuesday nights. That is what worked.
choices.outcome: You take them to your Tuesday Meet-the-People Session. One stays until midnight writing a letter that argues the case, and you recognise the look. The paper is not revised.

choices.text: Send them to your volunteers instead of you.
choices.outcome: Your longest-serving volunteer mentors all three for six weeks and refuses lunch every time. All three win their seats. None of their victory speeches mentions the volunteer.

title: The Improvement Plan
body: Last year's D means an improvement plan: three targets, six months, then a review. Miss the targets, or get another D, and you'll be asked to leave. Your reporting officer asks you to sign it, and explains, twice, that signing means you've read it, not that you agree.

choices.text: Sign it, and meet every target.
choices.outcome: You meet all three targets, two of them early. The review takes eleven minutes and ends with the word "encouraging". The plan is closed, and so, for now, is the question of you leaving.

choices.text: Ask HR for a transfer before the review.
choices.outcome: HR finds you a post in another division, under a director who has never read your file. The plan closes when you move. You start again, among people who don't know you yet.

choices.text: Dispute the D, in writing.
choices.outcome: Your reply runs to four pages and is filed with the plan. It doesn't change the grade. It does change your reporting officer, who now keeps notes of every meeting with you.

variants.body: Last year's D means an improvement plan: targets to meet in six months, then a review, and if it goes badly you'll be asked to leave. The plan comes on version 4.1 of HR's template, which has a new 150-word box for "Officer's Reflections" and a tick saying you helped write the plan. Someone has ticked it for you.

choices.text: Fill in the reflections, then meet every target.
choices.outcome: Your reflections come to exactly 150 words, because the box won't take more. You meet the targets two months early. Version 4.2 of the template uses your plan, without your name, as its example.

choices.text: Ask HR for a posting before the review.
choices.outcome: HR moves you to another division before the review is even scheduled. The plan closes as "Officer Transferred", which the HR system counts as a success.

choices.text: Use the reflections box to disagree, politely.
choices.outcome: You disagree in 150 words, politely. At the review your reporting officer has clearly read them twice, and asks you something that isn't on the template: what would you change?

variants.body: Last year's appraisal was a D, so your reporting officer is putting you on an improvement plan. It arrives by email: six targets for the next six months. An HR officer you've never met is copied in, because if you miss the targets, the next conversation is about you leaving. The email's subject line is "Supporting your growth".

choices.text: Hit every target, and keep proof of each one in writing.
choices.outcome: Six months, six targets, six emails confirming each one was met. The HR officer replies to the last one, "Noted, thanks", and closes the plan. You have never been so well documented.

choices.text: Ask HR for a transfer to another division.
choices.outcome: HR agrees so quickly it seems to have been expecting you. Your new division has never heard of you or your plan, which is exactly what you wanted.

choices.text: Reply to each target, explaining why it's unfair.
choices.outcome: Your reply is longer than the plan. The HR officer reads all of it, carefully, and now knows exactly who you are. The plan stays as it was.

variants.body: Last year's D comes with an improvement plan, and the plan comes with a deadline: six months to meet its targets, then a review that decides whether you stay. It arrives as a form in the HR system. Your reporting officer has ticked four boxes and written one sentence. If you don't acknowledge it within five working days, the system acknowledges it for you.

choices.text: Acknowledge it, and work through the four boxes.
choices.outcome: All four boxes are done by the review. The system marks the plan "Completed" in green, then asks you to rate the experience out of five. You give it a four.

choices.text: Ask HR for a transfer before day five.
choices.outcome: HR moves faster than the system. By the time the plan acknowledges itself, you've been moved, and it's addressed to a job you no longer have.

choices.text: Fill the comments box, all 2,000 characters of it.
choices.outcome: You use exactly 2,000 characters; the box won't take more. Your reporting officer reads every one, books a meeting room, and asks, for the first time, what you think is going wrong.

variants.body: Last year's D means an improvement plan: three objectives for the next six months, then a review that decides whether you stay. The objectives are, in order: to improve, to show that you've improved, and to "take ownership of your improvement journey". Your reporting officer got them from a leadership course.

choices.text: Improve, show it, and own the journey.
choices.outcome: You improve, report it in a monthly email, and own the journey in a slide. All three objectives are marked "Met", and the leadership course asks if it can use your slide.

choices.text: Ask to continue the journey in another division.
choices.outcome: HR arranges a transfer within the month. Your new reporting officer has never heard of an improvement journey, and on your first day asks you to fix a spreadsheet instead.

choices.text: Ask, in writing, how you'll know the journey has ended.
choices.outcome: Your one-page question is filed with the plan and never answered. At the review, the third objective has quietly disappeared, and the first two are marked "Met".

variants.body: Last year's D has started an improvement plan, and its first meeting is in a room booked under "Catch-up". Your reporting officer, an HR partner and a printed copy of your objectives are waiting. Fail the review in six months, or get another D, and you will be asked to leave.

choices.text: Agree the targets in the room, and meet them.
choices.outcome: You agree all four targets before the meeting ends, which nobody expected, and meet them in five months. The HR partner closes the file and stamps it, with some ceremony, "Closed".

choices.text: Ask HR, quietly, about a transfer.
choices.outcome: The HR partner slips you a card on the way out. Within a month you are in another division, and the room booked under "Catch-up" is booked by somebody else.

choices.text: Ask for the reasons for the D, in writing, first.
choices.outcome: The reasons arrive three weeks later, two pages long. You agree with one of them. Your reporting officer, reading your reply, agrees with one of yours.

variants.body: Last year's D means an improvement plan, and this year's plans come with a "buddy", an officer from another division who checks on you once a month. The targets are due in six months; miss them, or get another D, and you will be asked to leave. Your buddy is younger than you, and very kind about it.

choices.text: Meet the targets, with the buddy's monthly check-ins.
choices.outcome: You meet the targets, and your buddy's final report is so warm that HR asks whether the two of you are related. The plan is closed.

choices.text: Ask HR to move you before the first check-in.
choices.outcome: HR moves you before the buddy's first visit. The buddy is assigned to someone else, and sends you a cheerful message wishing you luck.

choices.text: Tell the buddy, politely, that the D was wrong.
choices.outcome: Your buddy listens, writes it all down, and puts it in the monthly report. Nothing changes on paper. Your reporting officer starts asking for your view in meetings, which is something.

variants.body: The improvement plan for last year's D arrives as a spreadsheet: five targets, each with a weighting, the weightings adding up to a hundred per cent. In six months a review decides whether you stay, and another D decides it for you. Someone has already filled in the column headed "Progress" with zeros.

choices.text: Fill in the progress column, one target at a time.
choices.outcome: By the review every row says a hundred per cent, and the spreadsheet turns itself green. HR closes the plan, and keeps your spreadsheet as a template.

choices.text: Ask for a transfer before the first update is due.
choices.outcome: HR moves you to another division before the first update. The spreadsheet stays behind, all zeros, in a shared folder nobody opens.

choices.text: Add a column of your own, headed "Context".
choices.outcome: Your column runs longer than the rest of the spreadsheet put together. The review reads it, keeps the D, and quietly drops one of the five targets.

comply: Another improvement plan arrives on the same template, and you do what you did with the first: sign, meet, file.
Another improvement plan is marked Met and added to your file, which HR now describes as "a pattern".
The improvement plan comes round again, and you sign where it says acknowledgement and work to its dates.
Another improvement plan brings the same three objectives in a different order, and you clear them in the old one.
You meet the new improvement plan's objectives a month early, and the review is cancelled for lack of material.
The improvement plan arrives with last time's comments still in its margin, and you work through it in the same order.
move: Another improvement plan arrives, and you ask for a posting again; HR still has your last request on file.
HR moves you before the new improvement plan's first review and closes it as "Officer Transferred", as before.
HR processes your transfer request faster than last time, which it treats as a sign of maturity.
A new improvement plan, then a new division, and a new reporting officer who reads your file from the back.
You are posted out within the month, and the improvement plan is closed by a system that records you as "Moved On".
Your transfer is approved before the improvement plan's review is booked, by an HR officer who recognises your name.
contest: Another improvement plan arrives, and you reply to it in writing, at the same length as last time.
Your written reply to the new improvement plan is filed beside the old one, and the review moves to a larger room.
Another improvement plan, another four-page reply, and HR opens a second folder because the first is full.
You answer the new improvement plan point by point, and your reporting officer now writes everything down, in pen.
Your written reply cites the previous plan by paragraph number, which nobody on the panel can find.
The new improvement plan comes with a box for your comments, and your comments come with an annex.

title: A Word from the Whip
body: Last year your work as an MP was graded a D. So the Party Whip would like a word, over kopi, about your attendance, your ward, and a speech the papers called "brief". Nobody says "improvement plan", but everyone knows that's what this is: another D and your time in politics is over.

choices.text: Promise to do better, and then do it.
choices.outcome: You speak in three debates and visit every block in your ward twice. The Whip's next note to you is one line long. It says "Good."

choices.text: Ask to move to a committee where you'd be useful.
choices.outcome: You're moved to a Government Parliamentary Committee that meets at eight in the morning. It turns out you're a morning person now.

choices.text: Explain, politely, that your ward comes first.
choices.outcome: The Whip agrees that the ward comes first, and points out that Parliament is also, technically, somewhere you're meant to be.

comply: The Whip has another word over kopi, and you promise again to do better, and again you do.
Another word from the Whip, then three more debates, every block visited twice, and a note that says "Good."
You are reminded, kindly, that the House sits on Mondays, and after that you are there for every one.
The Whip's word is shorter this time, and your attendance afterwards is longer.
move: The Whip has another word, and you ask to move committees again; there is one that meets at seven.
You move to another committee that meets at an hour that suits nobody, so attendance is excellent.
Another word from the Whip, another committee, and your diary now holds more committees than days.
The Whip finds you a committee again, and you find, again, that you are useful on it.
contest: The Whip has another word, you explain again that the ward comes first, and the Whip agrees again, in writing.
Over kopi you repeat that the ward comes first, and the Whip repeats that Parliament is also somewhere you are meant to be.
Another word from the Whip, and another polite reply about the ward, filed with the others.
You tell the Whip the ward comes first, and your attendance record agrees, which is the difficulty.

title: The Bed Crunch
body: Public hospitals are over ninety per cent full, and emergency waiting times are in the papers again. You've been asked for a paper on transitional care: beds outside the hospitals for patients who are well enough to leave but have nowhere ready to go. The Minister wants something to announce.

choices.text: Recommend more transitional beds, and say where the nurses will come from.
choices.outcome: Your paper has a section on nurses that nobody asked for and everybody quotes. The beds are approved. Staffing them is, as you said it would be, the hard part.

choices.text: Recommend the beds, and leave the nurses to a later paper.
choices.outcome: The beds are approved quickly. A later paper, not yours, discovers there aren't enough nurses, and cites yours as "an important first step".

choices.text: Recommend better discharge planning instead.
choices.outcome: It's the right answer and the less announceable one. The hospitals like it. The press office asks whether there's a version with a number in it.

title: The Premiums
body: Premiums for MediShield Life, the national health insurance everyone pays into, are going up, and the actuaries have done the sums: the increase is what it is. Your job is to decide how it's put to the public: all at once or over several years, and with how much subsidy shown beside it. Whatever you choose, someone will add it up.

choices.text: Present the full number, with the subsidies next to it.
choices.outcome: The increase is large, the subsidies are larger for the people who need them, and the slide says both. It's the least comfortable slide in the deck, and the only one nobody later has to correct.

choices.text: Phase it over three years, so no single year looks large.
choices.outcome: Each year looks reasonable. Within a week somebody adds the three years together, in a letter to the newspaper, with a table in it.

choices.text: Ask the actuaries to walk you through their assumptions first.
choices.outcome: Two days in a room with the actuaries. You come out understanding medical cost inflation better than anyone in your division, and slightly worried about it.

title: The Waiting Time
body: A resident's post about a six-hour wait at a hospital emergency department, with photographs, has four thousand shares and one factual error. Hospitals are your ministry's business, so on Sunday, at a community event, you will be asked about it whether you prepare or not. Whatever you say will be clipped.

choices.text: Visit the emergency department on Saturday night, unannounced.
choices.outcome: You sit in the waiting area for two hours. Nobody recognises you, which tells you something about the waiting area and something else about you.

choices.text: Answer on Sunday with the figures, and correct the error.
choices.outcome: Your figures are accurate and the error is corrected. The resident's reply to your answer is shared more widely than the answer.

choices.text: Say the wait was too long, and stop there.
choices.outcome: It was too long, and you say so in nine words. The clip is on the evening news. Your colleagues' faces suggest you used about eight words too many.

title: The Dormitory Standards
body: Your division has drafted new standards for migrant worker dormitories: fewer beds to a room, more toilets, better ventilation, more space per worker. The dormitory operators have written to say they'll pass the cost on to employers. The employers have written to say they won't absorb it. You decide what holds.

choices.text: Hold the standards, and phase the deadline.
choices.outcome: The standards hold. The deadline moves twice, in writing, with reasons. Two years later the rooms are measurably less crowded. It isn't a headline, and that's the point.

choices.text: Hold the standards and the deadline.
choices.outcome: Three operators complain about you, by name, to three different people. The rooms are less crowded on schedule.

choices.text: Soften the space requirement for existing dormitories.
choices.outcome: Everyone is relieved, including you, briefly. New dormitories meet the new standard. The old ones keep to the old one, for longer than anyone said they would.

title: The Wage Ladder
body: Your division is extending the Progressive Wage Model, the ladder of minimum wages tied to skills, to another sector. The union wants the ladder steeper, so pay rises faster. The employers want it longer, so pay rises slowly. The workers in the sector, when you finally meet some, want to know when.

choices.text: Back the steeper ladder.
choices.outcome: The ladder ends up steeper than the employers wanted and gentler than the union asked for. In tripartite talks, where government, unions and employers settle wages together, that's a win for everyone and a story for nobody.

choices.text: Broker the longer, gentler ladder.
choices.outcome: Everyone signs. The first rung is lower than you'd hoped. You tell yourself it's a ladder, and ladders get climbed.

choices.text: Take both versions back to the workers, and ask.
choices.outcome: They choose the steeper one and ask for it sooner. You write that down exactly, and it goes into the paper sent upstairs. Workers' own words rarely get that far.

title: The Retirement Age
body: The retirement and re-employment ages are going up again, in steps, by law, and your ministry must explain it. At a dialogue for older workers, your slides are excellent. The first question, from a cleaner in the second row, is not on any of them, and the room is watching how you handle it.

choices.text: Answer her question, not the slides.
choices.outcome: Her question was whether she could keep her job if her knees could not. You answer it properly, which takes the rest of the session. The slides go home unshown.

choices.text: Take the question offline, and follow up.
choices.outcome: Your office follows up within a week, with a contact at her employer and a scheme she had not heard of. She never learns who sent it. That is fine.

choices.text: Ask the union representative beside you to take it.
choices.outcome: He answers it well, with a detail about re-employment contracts you did not know. The photograph in the newsletter is of him, answering it.

title: The Classification
body: HDB, the government's housing board, is planning a new estate, and you have to decide which of its projects are Standard, Plus or Prime. The label decides how long owners must live there and what they repay when they sell. You have a map, a set of criteria, and three neighbouring blocks that are, in every way a resident would notice, identical.

choices.text: Apply the criteria exactly, and let the line fall where it falls.
choices.outcome: The line falls between two of the three blocks. Years from now, two neighbours on the same corridor will have different rules for selling the same kind of flat, and both will know exactly why.

choices.text: Move the line so it follows the road.
choices.outcome: The road makes a tidy boundary, and the criteria get a footnote. Nobody reads footnotes, until somebody does.

choices.text: Write a note on the three blocks, and send it up.
choices.outcome: Your note asks a question nobody wanted asked. It's answered eventually, in a way you can live with, by someone more senior who takes the credit for the question.

title: Ninety-Nine Years
body: A residents' committee from a 1970s estate built by HDB, the government's housing board, has written in. Their leases are ninety-nine years long and about half used up. The letter is polite, well researched, and asks one question: what happens to their flats when the lease runs out. The answer is in the policy. They've read the policy.

choices.text: Meet them, and explain it in person.
choices.outcome: Two hours at a void deck, the shaded open space under one of their blocks. You explain the policy, and then you listen to what it means to them. That's a different conversation, and a longer one.

choices.text: Reply in writing, accurately and kindly.
choices.outcome: Your letter is accurate and kind. It's pinned on the noticeboard beside the lift, where everyone reads it and most people believe it.

choices.text: Invite them to the consultation on redevelopment.
choices.outcome: They come, all eleven of them, with a folder. Their folder is better organised than yours.

title: The Million-Dollar Flat
body: A second-hand public housing flat in an older estate has sold for one and a half million dollars, and the headline makes it sound as if every flat will. It was an unusually good flat; the headline does not say so. Housing is your ministry's job, and your phone has begun to buzz in the rhythm of a question you will have to answer.

choices.text: Point out, with numbers, how rare such sales are.
choices.outcome: The numbers are correct and reassuring. The comments under the article are neither.

choices.text: Say what the government is doing about supply.
choices.outcome: You list the new flat launches. The answer is solid and forgettable. On this subject, forgettable counts as a success.

choices.text: Say you understand why people are worried, and mean it.
choices.outcome: You do mean it, it shows, and the clip travels. A colleague says, kindly, that understanding is not a policy. You think it is a start.

title: The Merger List
body: Fewer children are born every year, so some schools must merge, and you're drawing up the list. Every school on it will lose its name or its building. Every school on it also has an alumni association, a school song, and a former principal who is still alive and writes letters.

choices.text: Draw the list on the numbers.
choices.outcome: The list is defensible, line by line. The letters arrive line by line too, many of them beautifully written, and all of them signed.

choices.text: Keep the oldest names, whatever the numbers say.
choices.outcome: The old names survive. Two newer schools with better numbers don't, and their students will remember the year their school was described as "consolidated".

choices.text: Propose that merged schools keep both names.
choices.outcome: The names are hyphenated. The school songs aren't, and the first combined assembly is, by every account, loud.

title: The Banding
body: Under Full Subject-Based Banding, students in the same class take different subjects at different levels, so a school's timetable no longer fits inside its classes. A principal has written to the ministry to say the school's teachers are now, in effect, air traffic controllers. The ministry's reply is yours to decide.

choices.text: Fund the timetabling software the principal asked for.
choices.outcome: The software mostly works. The teachers are now air traffic controllers with radar, which they say is an improvement.

choices.text: Send a guidebook and a hotline number.
choices.outcome: The guidebook is thorough and the hotline is staffed. The principal's reply thanks you for both, in a tone you'll remember.

choices.text: Spend a week in the school, and find out.
choices.outcome: You spend a week with a timetable on a wall the size of a car park, and come back with three changes that fit on one page. They work.

title: The PSLE Question
body: You are hosting a dialogue for parents on "the joy of learning". The first question is about how the PSLE, the exam at the end of primary school, is scored, and the second about tuition. The third is from a twelve-year-old, brought along by a parent, who wants to know why there is an exam at all. The room is waiting to see whose question you answer first.

choices.text: Answer the twelve-year-old first.
choices.outcome: Your answer is honest, and does not entirely defend the exam. The child nods. Several parents write it down, and you cannot tell whether that is a good sign.

choices.text: Take the questions in order.
choices.outcome: The scoring, tuition, and then, briefly, the child, who by now has been taken outside for a drink.

choices.text: Explain how the PSLE is scored, carefully, with the chart.
choices.outcome: Everyone in the room understands the chart. Nobody in the room is reassured by it. You suspect the chart was never the problem.

title: The Ask

asker.text: {peer}, who joined the service with you,
asker.yes: {peer} says you're owed one, and writes it in a notebook you've seen before.
asker.no: {peer} takes it well, and has asked someone else by lunchtime.

asker.text: {peer}, who got the director's post in the reorganisation instead of you,
asker.yes: {peer} says that makes the two of you even, and you both know it doesn't.
asker.no: {peer} says that's fair, and reminds you, lightly, which of you got the post.

asker.yes: {junior} thanks you twice, the second time when nobody else is around to hear it.
asker.no: {junior} nods, and doesn't ask you for anything else for some months.

asker.text: {junior}, who once proofread your annexes until 1:20am,
asker.yes: {junior} thanks you once, and you understand it's for the annexes as well.
asker.no: {junior} says that's fine, in very nearly the tone you used at 1:20am.

asker.text: {junior}, whom you once sent home before a deadline,
asker.yes: {junior} thanks you, and leaves on time that evening, which you also take as thanks.
asker.no: {junior} says that's fine, and leaves on time, which you take as the reply.

asker.yes: {senior} remembers it in the meeting that decides your grade, the only room where it counts.
asker.no: {senior} says that's perfectly fine, in the way the word is used upstairs.

want.text: a reference for a two-year posting to the Budget Division
want.a: You write three paragraphs, all of them true, and send them before midnight.
want.b: You write three good paragraphs, and copy in two people who'll remember that you wrote them.
want.c: You explain that a reference from you would read as a favour, because it would be one.

want.text: a second read of a paper that goes up at nine tomorrow
want.a: You read it twice and send back three comments, all of them fair, at 11:40pm.
want.b: You send back three comments, and mention at the morning meeting that you looked it over.
want.c: You say you can't do it justice tonight. It's true, and no help to the paper.

want.text: someone to take {asker.their} place at a Saturday dialogue session in Jurong
want.a: You spend the Saturday in Jurong with forty residents and a microphone that works half the time.
want.b: You take the Saturday session. Its photograph goes in the division newsletter, with you in front.
want.c: You keep your Saturday. The session goes ahead with nobody senior there, and is written up as "intimate".

snag.text: Your own paper is due the same week, and isn't finished.
HR sent round a reminder about conflicts of interest this morning, in bold.
Someone else on your floor asked you for the same thing an hour ago.
Nobody else has asked you for anything all week.

body: {Asker} stops you by the lift and asks you for a favour: {want}. Saying yes takes time. Saying no will be remembered. {snag}

choices.text: Say yes, and do it properly.
choices.outcome: {want.a} {asker.yes}

choices.text: Say yes, and make sure it's seen.
choices.outcome: {want.b} {asker.yes}

choices.text: Say no, and say why.
choices.outcome: {want.c} {asker.no}

title: The Ribbon

occasion.text: the handover of the new lifts at Blk 412
the reopening of the hawker centre after renovation
the opening of a rooftop garden on the multi-storey car park
the launch of a fitness corner first planned six years ago

host.where: is waiting at the ribbon with the scissors
host.give: Hand {grassroots} the scissors. It was {grassroots.their} work.
host.saw: {grassroots} mentions it to every residents' committee in the ward by Monday.
host.left: {grassroots} walks you to the car without a word, and that says enough.
host.gave: {grassroots}, the {grassroots.title}, cuts the ribbon slowly, to applause that is mostly for {grassroots.them}, and keeps the scissors.

host.text: {mp}, the MP for the next ward,
host.where: has come with a spare pair of scissors, hoping to share the photograph
host.give: Hand {mp} the scissors, and stand at the back.
host.saw: {mp} leaves halfway, and is in none of the photographs.
host.left: {mp} stays for the rest of it, and is in every photograph.
host.gave: {mp} cuts the ribbon. The newsletter's photograph is of {mp}, captioned with the name of your ward, and the Whip asks you why.

host.where: is waiting by the ribbon with a camera
host.give: Ask {journalist.formal} to photograph the residents, not you.
host.saw: {journalist.formal} files three paragraphs about it, and all three are accurate.
host.left: {journalist.formal} photographs you leaving. It is the photograph that runs.
host.gave: The photograph that runs is of four residents and a pair of scissors. It is the best one the paper prints that month, and you are not in it.

snag.text: Twenty minutes in, it starts to rain on the speeches.
snag.stay: You stay through the rain and the speeches, and shake every wet hand there is.
snag.go: You cut the ribbon under someone else's umbrella and are gone before the second speech.

snag.text: A resident has brought a petition about the bus stop, and a folding chair.
snag.stay: You sit beside the folding chair and read the petition, which has 212 signatures and one good idea.
snag.go: You accept the petition with both hands, pass it to an aide with one, and leave.

snag.text: The ribbon is the wrong colour. The right one is stuck in traffic on the expressway.
snag.stay: You wait forty minutes for the van and talk to everyone in the queue, and everyone is in the queue.
snag.go: You cut the wrong ribbon. Nobody minds except the person who ordered the right one.

snag.text: You are due across the ward in fifteen minutes.
snag.stay: You stay, and reach the next event as it is packing up, apologising mainly to the chairs.
snag.go: You cut the ribbon on time and are across the ward in fourteen minutes, which the driver mentions.

body: Today's ribbon is at {occasion}, and as the ward's MP you are there to cut it. {Host} {host.where}. {snag} Residents will notice how long you stay and who gets the credit.

choices.text: Stay to the end, and talk to everyone.
choices.outcome: {snag.stay} {host.saw}

choices.text: Cut the ribbon, smile, and go.
choices.outcome: {snag.go} {host.left}

choices.text: {host.give}
choices.outcome: {host.gave}

title: Reply All

sent.text: your draft reply, with your notes to yourself still in square brackets
sent.fix: Your correction is two lines long. The square brackets are discussed for a week, and then quoted, fondly, at the division retreat.

sent.text: last year's figures, attached instead of this year's
sent.fix: Your correction attaches the right file and the words "with apologies". By then, three people have already pasted last year's figures into something.

sent.text: the words "Is this serious?" in a reply meant for one person
sent.fix: Your correction explains that the line wasn't meant to go round. By then it's the most widely read thing you've ever written.

to.joke: The joke lands. Two people you've never spoken to say hello in the lift the following week.
Forty agencies ignore the joke. One replies all to ask to be taken off the list, and the whole thing starts again.
The Minister's office doesn't reply. By Monday your joke has been forwarded back to you three times, without comment, which is a comment.

noticed.text: {peer} messages you within the minute: "Check your sent folder."
{senior} replies to all, "Noted, thanks," which keeps the thread alive into the weekend.
Nobody says anything. Everyone has read it.

body: At 4:52pm on a Friday, you accidentally send {to} {sent}. Email recalls rarely work, and on Monday everyone will remember whose name was on it. {noticed}

choices.text: Send a short correction to everyone, now.
choices.outcome: {sent.fix}

choices.text: Recall it, and hope.
choices.outcome: The recall reaches the people who hadn't opened it. Everyone else receives a second email, saying you would like to recall the first.

choices.text: Reply all once more, with an apology and a joke.
choices.outcome: {to.joke}

title: The Box Marked Successor
body: The Public Service Division, which makes the service's top appointments, asks every Permanent Secretary to name a successor, in confidence, on a form with one box. Your two Deputy Secretaries are the obvious names. One would carry on everything you have built. The other is sharper, and would quietly undo half of it.

choices.text: Name the one who would undo it.
choices.outcome: You write the sharper name, and sign before you can reconsider. The Public Service Division thanks you for your "candour", the word it uses when someone has surprised it.

choices.text: Name the one who would carry it on.
choices.outcome: You write the loyal name, and the Public Service Division agrees within a week. Everything you built will be safe for years, including the parts that shouldn't be.
